The Party Shaping Spain’s Election Isn’t Even on the Ballot

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov.
  • Sánchez called elections after failing to get emergency legislation aimed at tackling Spain’s housing crisis through parliament in October.
  • Catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov. 29. Junts per Catalunya, the separatist party that supported Sánchez to form a minority government in 2023, turned against him last year to fend off a fresh far-right rival—ultimately forcing the early vote.

Sánchez called elections after failing to get emergency legislation aimed at tackling Spain’s housing crisis through parliament in October. The conservative People’s Party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the center-right Junts all voted against the package.

Catalonia’s independence movement is moving to the right, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez might pay the price in snap parliamentary elections on Nov. 29. Junts per Catalunya, the separatist party that supported Sánchez to form a minority government in 2023, turned against him last year to fend off a new far-right rival—ultimately forcing the early vote.

Sánchez called elections after failing to get emergency legislation aimed at tackling Spain’s housing crisis through parliament in October. The conservative People’s Party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the center-right Junts all voted against the package.

It was the latest example of Junts going against the minority government’s initiatives. When party head Carles Puigdemont revealed that Junts would revoke its backing and move into the opposition last year, he blamed Sánchez’s Socialist Workers’ Party for broken promises. But the pro-independence party is also facing a growing threat at home in Catalonia.

According to recent reports, that threat is Aliança Catalana—a far-right, separatist party led by Sílvia Orriols, the mayor of the small town of Ripoll. Orriols founded Aliança in 2020 after breaking with another separatist party; its platform combines a demand for Catalan independence with hard-line hostility toward immigration and Islam. She pushed for a tougher approach to immigration after the 2017 Barcelona attacks, carried out by a terror cell based in Ripoll.

In a recent development, unlike Junts, Aliança has elected not to stand in the Nov. 29 national elections, refusing to take part based on its Catalonian separatism. “We are not thinking about influencing Madrid, and that’s part of the foundation of Aliança,” said the party’s press chief, Eduard Berraondo.

It has been revealed that polling right now points to a right-wing majority. The PP leads with 31.2 percent of the vote, with the Socialists at 29.3 percent, and Vox at 18 percent as of Nov. 24, according to newspaper Ara’s polling average. Together, the PP and Vox are projected to win around 190 seats, above the 176 needed for a majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Only the state-run Center for Sociological Studies pollster, which critics say favors the government, puts the Socialists ahead.

So, although Aliança isn’t on the ballot, its rapid rise is reshaping Spanish politics.

According to recent reports, the party’s hard line on immigration and Islam has pushed Junts to the right, making the party ever less likely to partner with the Socialists. Aliança’s voters could help decide where Catalonia’s right-wing vote goes: back to Junts, across to Vox, or nowhere at all. Finally, the party’s growing popularity suggests a deeper shift among Catalan independence supporters, away from progressivism and toward a more exclusionary view of who counts as Catalan.

Aliança has risen rapidly in Catalonia. The far-right party won just two of 135 seats in the Catalan parliamentary elections in 2024, but the latest survey from the Catalan government’s polling agency, the Centre d’Estudis d’Opinió (CEO), projects that the party would capture between 23 and 25 seats if regional elections were held now. Junts, which holds 35 seats, would fall to between 18 and 20.

According to recent reports, catalonia’s next regional elections must be held by late June 2028. Almost 1 in 5 people who voted for Junts in 2024 now say they would back Aliança—but a majority of those wavering respondents still ranked Junts as their second choice.

Aliança’s message lands with voters anxious about rapid population growth, crime, and stretched public services. Around 18 percent of its supporters say they would vote for Vox on Nov. 29, according to the CEO. This matters in Madrid, where each seat that Junts loses weakens the leverage that once made it a kingmaker.

According to recent reports, junts is responding to Aliança’s rise by shifting to the right. The party has demanded that Madrid hand Catalonia control over immigration, backed bans on the burqa and niqab in public spaces, and pushed for tougher rules on repeat criminal offenders. The party has also proposed making immigrants wait 10 years after registering as residents before they can apply for subsidized housing, more than three times the current maximum.

Sources indicate that catalonia elects 48 members of Spain’s national parliament; Junts holds seven of those seats. In return for the party’s support after the 2023 election, the Socialists pushed through an amnesty law covering those involved in the 2017 Catalan independence push, including Puigdemont, who at the time served as Catalonia’s president and fled to Belgium to avoid arrest. The Supreme Court lifted his arrest warrant in October, clearing the way for his return.

Recent findings suggest that junts has ruled out backing either Sánchez or the PP’s party leader for prime minister, though it has left the door open to supporting a different Socialist candidate. Competing with Aliança for allegiance in Catalonia, it has little room to prop up a left-wing government. With a PP-Vox majority, that might not matter. But if the right-wing vote falls short, Spain’s government could once again hang on a handful of Catalan votes.

The CEO expects Junts to win just four or five parliamentary seats in the snap elections, while Vox could more than double its share of Catalonia’s seats—from two seats to five or six. Some of those votes might come from Aliança supporters.

“From Nov. 29, a dual voter will emerge: someone who votes Aliança in municipal and Catalan elections, and Vox in Spanish ones,” stated Xavier Torrens, a professor of political science at the University of Barcelona.

Vox and Aliança are opposed when it comes to the question of Catalonia’s independence, but on immigration, they speak the same language.

In a recent development, “Many people vote Vox because they reject immigration, feel unsafe, or believe immigrants take a large share of public benefits. Aliança says the same,” said Xavier Rius, a Catalan journalist and the author of a book on Aliança.

Berraondo rejected a direct comparison between his party and Vox, insisting that their positions overlap only on immigration and law and order and that Aliança does not share Vox’s opposition to abortion and gay rights.

It has been revealed that still, Aliança might see a PP-Vox victory as good news for its future. “Imagine you think that if the PP and Vox win the elections in November, they could start the dirty job of changing the immigration rules,” Berraondo said. “Then you can take advantage of it if you are in government in Catalonia in 2028.”.

According to recent reports, this political convergence would once have been unthinkable. The Catalan independence movement defined itself against the Spanish nationalism that Vox represents and long prided itself on being progressive, inclusive, and pro-European. Center-right parties joined the independence push in the 2010s, but Aliança is the first far-right separatist party to gain traction in Catalonia.

So, how did a far-right party emerge from the movement, and why now? Part of the answer lies in 2017. That October, Catalonia’s pro-independence government held a referendum that Spain’s Constitutional Court had declared illegal. Puigdemont signed a declaration of independence and then days later declared that he asked parliament to suspended it. Weeks later, Madrid suspended Catalonia’s autonomy, and the movement’s leaders were jailed or fled abroad.

For many Junts supporters, the promise that independence was within reach proved hollow. Puigdemont’s about-face and rush to negotiate with Madrid seemed to reveal that the party prioritized its political leverage over independence—a perception later reinforced when Junts backed Sanchez’s government and demanded amnesty for its leaders rather than any move toward independence.

Recent findings suggest that orriols, the Aliança leader, has built her appeal on that sense of betrayal, casting the referendum moment as a deception and Puigdemont as a leader who lost his nerve. Voters who have switched allegiance from Junts to Aliança are, on average, around 56 years old, with nearly 89 percent supporting independence, according to the CEO. Their top concerns are immigration and insecurity. These are disappointed separatists—not newcomers to the cause.

Recent findings suggest that “Part of Junts’s electorate realized that the whole narrative about independence was just fluff, that they weren’t serious about it,” said Massimo Maoret, a professor at IESE Business School in Barcelona and a longtime observer of Catalan politics. Aliança, he added, has tapped into that feeling “together with anti-immigrant, and especially anti-Islamic, sentiment.”.

It has been revealed that further, as the cost of living rises, the concerns over affordable housing that brought down Sánchez’s government have also boosted the far-right party. Aliança “is winning an anti-system, anti-establishment vote, driven by people being fed up with the rising cost of living, the high cost of housing, and the poor functioning of public services such as rail transport,” Torrens said.

Aliança has drawn a connection between those issues and immigration, from pushing a debate over who counts as Catalan. For decades, the independence movement embraced a slogan popularized by Jordi Pujol, a former Catalan president: “Anyone who lives and works in Catalonia is Catalan.”.

Aliança takes a different line. “Aliança considers that only some of Catalonia’s inhabitants are Catalan, while the rest are immigrants settled in Catalonia but not Catalan,” Torrens said. Orriols has said that Muslims could not be Catalan because “they don’t integrate with the country’s culture and values.”.

It has been revealed that vox could unseat Pedro Sánchez in snap elections. How do you beat such an unusual party?

Why Spain’s Sánchez has succeeded while Britain’s Starmer floundered.

It has been revealed that the question is the extent to which Aliança is shaping the independence movement. Junts has already shifted toward some of Aliança’s positions on immigration—but Jordi Turull, Junts’s secretary-general, has warned that the far right “will do nothing but take us further from our goal of a prosperous and complete Catalan republic.”.

Josep Vila, the president of the Catalan National Assembly, a grassroots pro-independence organization, declined to say whether Aliança belonged to the movement. The group was “not concerned by the diversity of political options,” Vila wrote in an email, as long as they shared a strategy for independence.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Aliança’s base is broadening beyond the independence movement. According to the CEO, only 53 percent of its supporters now back independence, down from 62 percent late last year. Taken together, the data suggest a shift in priorities. For disillusioned separatists and newcomers alike, concerns about immigration, security, and the cost of living increasingly outweigh the question of independence.

In a recent development, in some ways, Catalonia seems to be following a familiar European script of an emergent far right—this time from within a separatist movement. Torrens makes a distinction between national-populist parties that took decades to break through, such as France’s National Rally, and those that do so within a few years, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, Portugal’s Chega, and Vox itself.

Industry observers note that aliança, he said, is on the fast track. The party’s first test comes in this week’s snap elections, when its supporters could shape the outcome. The bigger tests come later: municipal elections in May 2027 and the regional election by 2028. For now, Aliança seems to have shifted the Catalan independence movement’s center of gravity, as a movement that prided itself on building a Catalonia for all has absorbed an us-versus-them view of who belongs.

According to recent reports, the Nov. 29 vote will offer the first signs of how far that shift reaches beyond Catalonia. If Junts loses seats in Madrid, and especially if the PP and Vox win a majority on their own, then Catalan separatists could lose their leverage over Spain’s government for the first time in years. The irony is that some of Aliança’s own supporters might help sweep the nationalists in.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn analyzes President Trump's new executive orders targeting birth tourism and birthright citizenship, plus the legal battle with the ACLU and a Texas hospital settlement. Urbahn discusses the constitutional battles ahead.

A DC federal judge, previously dubbed by President Donald Trump as an "anti- Trump Hater," blocked Trump's second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship in a Wednesday ruling.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who was recently in Trump's crosshairs after ruling against efforts to shut down the Kennedy Center for renovations and add Trump's name to the cultural institution, issued a 67-page ruling striking down an August executive order that barred U.S. -born children whose parents are suspected terrorists or gang members, or children born through surrogacy to foreign parents, from citizenship eligibility.

Cooper's ruling comes months after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's initial executive order, signed on his first day back in office. The order attempted to deny birthright citizenship to U.S.-born children whose mothers were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor green card holders.

WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER.

According to recent reports, demonstrators hold up an anti-Trump sign outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, after the justices curbed nationwide injunctions in a case stemming from President Donald Trump's initial bid to end birthright citizenship. (ALEX WROBLEWSKI/AFP via Getty Images).

"As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out fresh exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws," Cooper ruled.

Trump's second executive order was already partially blocked on Sept. 2 by U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland, whose injunction protected U.S.-born children of mothers who were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents.

Cooper's ruling expanded protections beyond that class to include additional children born to certain foreign government and international organization employees, parents deemed "alien enemies" by the administration and foreign parents who used commercial surrogacy services in the U.S.

In a recent development, "The merits in this case are clear-cut. The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law," Cooper wrote.

It has been revealed that in addition to the Supreme Court's June ruling in Trump v. Barbara, Cooper referred to the high court's ruling in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which determined that a man born to Chinese immigrants was a protected U.S. citizen under the 14th Amendment.

SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS.

President Donald Trump speaks during a news conference in the James S. Brady Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on nationwide injunctions in litigation over his first birthright citizenship executive order. (Mehmet Eser/Middle East Images via AFP).

Cooper noted that Wong Kim Ark established narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship, including for children of foreign diplomats, children born aboard foreign public ships and children of enemy forces occupying American territory.

"While the Fourteenth Amendment may theoretically permit upcoming exceptions beyond those listed in Wong Kim Ark, Congress has not authorized any such exceptions," Cooper wrote.

In a recent development, cooper argued that membership in a terrorist organization alone does not satisfy the historical exception to birthright citizenship for children of enemy forces occupying U.S. territory. He criticized the Trump administration's contention that foreign invaders could occupy American territory without actually holding it as an "outside-the-box understanding" of what constitutes an occupation.

"To recap, a parent’s purported status as an alien enemy, standing alone, cannot strip a U.S.-born child of his right to birthright citizenship," Cooper wrote. "The alien-enemy exception, properly understood, applies only to children born to hostile enemy forces in temporarily occupied U.S. territory.".

In a recent development, cooper also rejected Trump's attempt to deny birthright citizenship to children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements involving foreign parents, finding that the circumstances of their birth do not exempt them from U.S. jurisdiction.

According to recent reports, "Indeed, foreign parents choose surrogacy arrangements in the United States precisely to have the child be governed by U.S. law and have the surrogacy process ‘supervised by a court.," Cooper wrote.

TRUMP TO ASK SUPREME COURT TO REHEAR BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CASE AFTER 'INSANE DECISION'.

It has been revealed that demonstrators gather outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on May 15, 2025, in support of birthright citizenship during litigation over President Donald Trump's first executive order narrowing citizenship eligibility for children born on U.S. soil. (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty).

He noted that, prior to Trump's second executive order, the State Department recognized the citizenship of children born on American soil regardless of whether they were born through surrogacy.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the decision and request that the executive order be temporarily enforced while the litigation works its way through the courts, a process that could take months.

"This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Obama attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis remarked in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court.".

Industry observers note that the Justice Department could seek temporary relief from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit or seek intervention from the Supreme Court. Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE WITH TIES TO ANTI-TRUMP CONSPIRACY THEORY HIT WITH MISCONDUCT COMPLAINT.

In addition to ruling against Trump's Kennedy Center renovation efforts, Cooper ruled that Trump's Department of Government Efficiency must turn over records requested in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.

Trump has called Cooper one of the "Radical Left Democrats.".

Cooper is also married to Amy Jeffress, who was Biden’s personal lawyer in 2025 and previously did some work for the Jan. 6 committee.

Breaking: China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2797 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.
  • NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.
  • Today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that LYLE J. GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.

NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.

How America Can Avert an Unnecessary Rivalry.

Lyle J. Goldstein and Nina Tannenwald.

Today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China. Policymakers point to China’s increasingly aggressive policies toward Taiwan, its massive military buildup, and its resistance to engaging in some arms control measures as evidence that Beijing has accepted the inevitability of such a race or is even pursuing one. Worried by intellectual frameworks that emphasize the likelihood of war between rival great powers, many U.S. leaders and analysts see little choice but for the United States to arm itself, too. But this thinking risks becoming a self-fulling prophecy. The major danger is that an unrestrained arms race increases the likelihood of war over Taiwan or even of a catastrophic nuclear exchange.

Industry observers note that but the pessimism about averting an arms race is misplaced. A nuclear arms race, in particular, is not a foregone conclusion—and the United States has real opportunities to curb one. Avoiding a nuclear arms race will require a broader approach than the two-pronged one Washington has recently favored: building up U.S. nuclear deterrence and seeking to force concessions from Beijing by imposing restrictions on trade and technology transfers. American leaders should instead look beyond traditional deterrence, which falls short because its threat-based approach tends to provoke competition over arms, and strive to establish a more fundamental strategic stability through a process of reciprocal de-escalation and compromise. China is likely to be amenable to reciprocal de-escalation: it has a long tradition of moderation in nuclear matters and, ultimately, Chinese leaders do not want a war over Taiwan.

There are recent signs that even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has often boasted about his distaste for compromise, sees the value of engagement. After two U.S.-Chinese bilateral summits this year, in October he suggested that his November trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin should focus on “denuclearization.” But Washington will have to become much more consistent in its rejection of an arms race, including by modifying its support for Taiwan and incorporating China into global arms control leadership. A nuclear arms race with China becomes inevitable only if Washington continues to believe it is.

According to recent reports, china is undoubtedly pursuing a military buildup, including investments in nuclear weapons. Between 2020 and 2025, China doubled the number of its nuclear warheads, from 300 to 600—a startling increase, although its arsenal remains small compared with the United States’ approximately 3,700 warheads. In 2021, researchers at the Federation of American Scientists announced that China was constructing 350 new nuclear missile silos in three vast sites in Xinjiang and Gansu provinces. Beijing is also pursuing substantial qualitative upgrades to its nuclear weapons, a push it showcased at an October 2025 military parade that unveiled a new sea-released ballistic missile, two new kinds of intercontinental ballistic missiles, a new air-launched hypersonic missile, and a new long-range hypersonic cruise missile.

Sources indicate that then, this July, the Chinese navy tested a submarine-released long-range ballistic missile that could carry nuclear weapons. This significant upcoming capability will allow China to launch long-range nuclear strikes that can reach the United States from protected waters near its own coastline rather than having to sail out into the Pacific. A recent editorial in a leading Chinese foreign affairs newspaper took the candid yet disturbing step of explicitly linking China’s rapid nuclear buildup to its desire to exert sovereignty over Taiwan. “The great cause of national reunification,” it asserted, “must rest on a solid, realistic foundation. That foundation is, first and foremost, hard power.” Although such overt nuclear saber rattling remains rare, the link between Beijing’s nuclear forces and the Taiwan concern stretches back over three decades and is also supported by the scholar Tong Zhao’s detailed analysis of China’s nuclear buildup in Foreign Affairs in May.

As China builds up its military, the perception that it is on a collision course with the United States over Taiwan—one that inevitably includes the risk of nuclear escalation—has become widespread in Washington. Taiwan, of course, appears to be an obvious flash point. The United States has long committed itself informally to defending the island while China seeks to unify with it, by force if necessary. In October, Army General Ronald Clark, the head of the U.S. Pacific Command, affirmed that his forces are actively readying for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan that could come as early as 2027.

According to recent reports, the Biden administration and both Trump administrations made some attempts to engage China over arms control and nuclear risk reduction. Trump proposed trilateral arms control talks that would include Russia, whereas the Biden administration pursued bilateral talks with China on strategic stability and nuclear risk reduction. But both presidents gave up after China consistently rejected engaging in sustained talks on nuclear matters. Beijing’s stance is that it has a small nuclear arsenal compared with the United States and Russia and that it is important to first establish trust and mutual reassurance about core interests.

Recent findings suggest that beyond China’s resistance to arms control, theories about power that are trendy in Washington reinforce the collision course mentality. Numerous realist scholars argue that a U.S.-Chinese rivalry and even a great-power war may be structurally difficult to avoid. The political scientist Graham Allison captured this pessimism in his influential 2017 book, Destined for War, which argued that a so-called Thucydides trap—when a rapidly rising power challenges the position of the dominant power, yielding war—would doom the United States and China to conflict.

China hawks, such as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, increasingly advocate an aggressive focus on “preparing for World War III” with China as a way to avoid it. In a July Upcoming York Times interview, Colby argued that the United States must “deny” China “the ability to seize and hold the key territory” of Taiwan, by enhancing U.S. deterrence with a massive military buildup. The next month, speaking at a military conference, Colby specified that such a buildup ought to put a greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons and the ability to fight a so-called limited nuclear war. The enemy, Colby stated, has “got to believe there’s some sense in which we would use” nuclear weapons. Toward this end, the United States is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, a new air-introduced cruise missile, and new nuclear-armed submarines and bombers, and accelerating the ambitious Golden Dome homeland missile defense project. Unlike earlier U.S. missile defenses, which were designed to intercept limited strikes by so called rogue states such as Iran and North Korea, the Golden Dome is intended to defend against massive Chinese or Russian attacks. But the prospect of losing its ability to retaliate against a U.S. first strike only gives Beijing more incentive to expand its nuclear arsenal.

Such a nuclear-heavy approach only prevents a war with China if nuclear deterrence succeeds. That puts a lot of eggs in the deterrence basket. And recent wars suggest that nuclear deterrence is becoming less effective. Russia’s nuclear threats have not coerced Ukraine into halting its strikes deep into Russian territory. Iran has proved willing to launch strikes against nuclear-armed Israel as well as U.S. bases and allies in the Middle East. What is most ominous, in May 2025, India and Pakistan crossed previous redlines and attacked each other’s homelands, something that mutual nuclear deterrence was supposed to prevent. Even if neither the United States nor China want nuclear war, a China determined to unify with Taiwan may not be intimidated by U.S. nuclear threats.

A recent study by Brown University’s Costs of War program found that the United States has already spent more than $3.4 trillion on its militarized rivalry with China over the last decade. Sustaining or ramping up this spending—which encompasses upcoming warships, aircraft, long-range missiles, drones, base upgrades, forward deployments, large military exercises, research and development, and new nuclear weapons—is infeasible in an era of ballooning national debt and expanding domestic needs.

In a recent development, one of the tragedies of an arms race is that neither party may actually want to pursue one. Despite its current arms buildup, Beijing has a long record of moderation in military and nuclear matters. For many decades, it has maintained a minimal nuclear deterrent and a no-first-use policy, and it did not use major military force to achieve strategic goals. Although it has long had access to the relevant technologies, China appears not to have produced or deployed tactical nuclear weapons. Chinese diplomats played a substantial role in coaxing Iran to accept the Obama administration’s 2015 nuclear deal and supported the UN’s relatively stringent sanctions on North Korea. And in the fall of 2022, according to then Secretary of State Antony Blinken and reporting by the Financial Times, China likely intervened diplomatically with the Kremlin to help stop Russia from using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. More broadly, China has embraced international law when it comes to war, playing a constructive role, for example, in removing chemical weapons from Syria in 2013.

Beijing’s inclination toward restraint has not disappeared completely, even as it upgrades its military. In November 2023, U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi agreed to renew lines of communication between their countries’ militaries that had been severed after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan the previous year. A year later, the two leaders affirmed that humans, not AI, must control the decision to use nuclear weapons. And in late 2025, Beijing released a white paper emphatically reiterating its support for nuclear arms control and has moved toward more transparency by publishing more information, including in English, about its military upgrades.

According to recent reports, chinese leaders clearly do not want a war over Taiwan. Publicly, they repeatedly emphasize that their goal is “peaceful unification” and “winning without fighting,” invoking the Chinese strategist Sun-tzu. Beijing’s longtime “one country, two systems” policy toward Taiwan—which would bring the island under Chinese sovereignty while allowing it substantial autonomy—leaves room for a negotiated solution. Last year, in an important analysis of China’s strategic ambitions, the scholars David Kang, Jackie Wong, and Zenobia Chan examined 12,000 articles and hundreds of speeches by Xi to argue that Beijing prioritizes regime stability and internal development over displacing the United States as a global military hegemon. Although China’s major, unannounced exercises around Taiwan earlier this month may constitute an exception, overall, Chinese military exercises near Taiwan over the last five years are consistent with this interpretation: many have reacted to perceived provocations, illustrate only medium-scale capabilities, and have generally had a performative quality, accompanied by extensive press coverage.

Sources indicate that there is still an opening for the United States and China to de-escalate. To achieve strategic stability, the two countries will need to make a concerted effort to defuse their security dilemma—the dynamic in which each side perceives the other’s defensive measures as aggressive. First, U.S. and Chinese leaders need to revive superpower summitry. Biden held only three face-to-face meetings with Xi on the sidelines of regional economic meetings. Although the May 2026 Beijing summit between Trump and Xi yielded no major breakthroughs, the meeting did improve the two leaders’ personal relationship; today, U.S.-Chinese tensions are lower than they were between 2021 and 2025. This progress suggests the great value of holding a regular, annual, multiday bilateral summit with a significant focus on nuclear arms control. Such meetings would give expert working groups time to methodically develop measures to reduce the risk of conflict. Just as important, the summits need to be long enough to leave room for unscripted conversations. At their first summit, in Geneva in November 1985, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev famously broke away from anxious bureaucrats and advisers for an impromptu walk—an encounter that helped establish a more constructive relationship.

In a recent development, the United States must also take concrete steps to reduce the chance of escalation in the Taiwan Strait. Above all, it should adhere more consistently to its “one China” policy—its position that Beijing is the sole legal government of China. More consistency would include limiting U.S. legislators’ trips to the island and downgrading U.S.-Taiwanese defense relations by, for example, holding meetings less frequently and at lower diplomatic levels. Washington should remind key allies such as Japan to proceed cautiously in terms of their rhetoric and military deployments. Such a restraint-oriented strategy would make it clear to Taiwan that independence is off the table, encouraging it to take a more accommodating approach that would lower the temperature with Beijing. If Washington were to agree to common-sense limitations on arms sales to Taiwan—such as refusing to sell Taiwan the surface-to-surface ballistic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), which can reach across the strait to the Chinese mainland—Beijing would likely reciprocate by scaling back its military exercises and related military deployments around the island. There are real incentives for Beijing to de-escalate. Doing so could improve relations with neighbors such as Japan, free up focus for domestic priorities, lower military spending, and limit the chance of war.

The Pentagon needs to demonstrate Washington’s intent to avoid war over Taiwan by gradually decreasing U.S. warship transits through the Taiwan Strait. Even more crucial, Washington should also substantially reduce U.S. military deployments in the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines and around Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Such deployments only exacerbate the security dilemma.

Exhibiting restraint does not mean the United States would be giving Taiwan away. The United States can continue to provide Taiwan with defensive arms (such as missile interceptors, artillery, drones, and mines) and harden U.S. bases in the region to provide stabilizing deterrence. But even if U.S. leaders publicly abjure direct military intervention to defend Taiwan—a rational step that would lower the risk of nuclear war—China will prefer negotiating with Taipei on the island’s autonomy over a bloody military showdown with Taiwanese forces. For their part, Taiwan’s leaders will likely accommodate themselves to limited self-governance under Chinese overall sovereignty. In the end, China’s main goal is to get Taiwan out of the U.S. sphere of influence. Chinese leaders’ major fear is not so much Taiwanese autonomy as the prospect of the island serving as a U.S. forward base—in Chinese parlance, “using Taiwan to contain China.”.

In a recent development, another crucial step would be to seek a multilateral pledge by all nuclear-armed states to employ nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack. Such a policy would reduce the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. China has long embraced such a no-first-use policy, but U.S. leaders have traditionally opposed it, believing that it might expose U.S. allies to conventional attack. The U.S. nuclear deterrent for allies, however, increasingly lacks credibility because the costs of starting a nuclear war would vastly outweigh the benefits. And after the collapse of traditional nuclear arms control, a mutual no-first-use policy offers a promising area of common ground between the United States and China. It would reinforce the existing no-first-use policies of China and India and implicitly acknowledge their leadership in the area of nuclear restraint, a virtue when newer nuclear states are chafing under the old Cold War superpowers’ dominance of arms control. This approach could even entice Beijing into a wider, more comprehensive process of bilateral or multilateral nuclear arms control.

Industry observers note that beyond these three major initiatives, the United States and China should sign an agreement to notify each other about their ballistic missile tests. Washington could also consider giving Beijing a larger role in nonproliferation efforts, for instance by affording China leadership roles in negotiations and inspection regimes in future nonproliferation arrangements. The U.S. arms control agenda with China should focus not only on offensive nuclear systems but also on missile defenses and tactical nuclear weapons, as well as AI technologies. And it would help if the United States evolved its own nuclear posture in the direction of restraint by reducing its warheads, warfighting capabilities, and alert posture.

Ultimately, the United States needs to get serious about reining in an arms race with China before its perception that one is apace becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. The two countries have a mutual interest in restraint. If Washington continues to overlook Beijing’s incentives to compromise—and the real signs that it is willing to do so—an arms race that, as of now, is mostly putative will become a reality. And a catastrophic war that could have been avoided could indeed become inevitable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that heritage Foundation chief economist E.J. Antoni blasts democratic socialist members of Congress for saying they want money out of politics while accepting campaign contributions from corporate executives and defense contractors.

Far-left lawmakers are facing accusations of hypocrisy for criticizing corporate influence in politics while accepting campaign contributions from influential executives in industries including defense and healthcare.

A latest investigation looking into Federal Election Commission filings found socialist-aligned candidates who pledged to reject corporate PAC contributions still took the cash from PAC's and corporate executives.

Sources indicate that "If you're taking money from them, at least be man enough to admit you're going to take the money," Rep.-elect Jerry Carl, R-Ala., told Fox News Digital in reference to Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich.

Recent findings suggest that filings first flagged by anti-DEI nonprofit 1792 Exchange were reviewed by Fox News Digital. They show Tlaib accepted checks in 2023 and 2025 totaling $10,600 from L3Harris executive defense contractor Faisal Munir, even after she authored an op-ed in 2025 criticizing lawmakers who financially benefit from the defense industry.

RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib speaks during the DWC x the Mamas’ Caucus hearing "Moms Pay the Price: The Republican Affordability Crisis" at the Rayburn House Office Building on April 28, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images for MomsRising).

Other Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members, such as, Reps.-elect Donavan McKinney, D-Mich., Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., and Darializa Avila Chevalier, D-N.Y., publicly pledged to reject corporate PAC contributions, according to End Citizens United. Yet all three took cash from PACs and corporate executives, as noted in the investigation.

While still candidates, however, they never specified if their pledge to reject corporate money also applies to the individuals running corporations and those outside PACs.

On her campaign website, Chevalier calls for banning super PAC money from elections, arguing that the political system "rewards the wealthy elite, corporations, and political machines over working people.".

Valdez, similarly, has criticized money in politics and blamed "AIPAC, crypto and AI" for "spending millions and millions of dollars" in "trying to influence the elections.".

McKinney denounced the campaign finance system on his website, arguing that it prevents elected officials from addressing voters' concerns.

Darializa Avila Chevalier, U.S. Democratic House candidate for Latest York, speaks at a Get Out The Vote rally at Kings Theater in Brooklyn, New York, on June 18, 2026, ahead of the state's primary election on June 23. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

'SQUAD' RAKES IN RECORD $2.35M WHILE SLAMMING THE DOOR ON COP DONATIONS.

Omar Tawakol, CEO of AI advertising platform Rembrand, contributed $13,600 to Tlaib, $7,000 to McKinney and $3,500 each to Valdez and Chevalier.

The initial investigation notes that 24 corporate executives contributed a combined $675,300 to DSA-endorsed congressional candidates during the two previous election cycles. 17 of those 24 contributed $126,300 directly to the DSA-endorsed candidates.

The other $549,000 went to three progressive political action committees: Justice Democrats, Leaders We Deserve and the Working Families Party PAC, which largely relies on money from corporate executives and other PACs which support the DSA candidates.

Industry observers note that justice Democrats contributed to Chevalier, Tlaib and Valdez, while Leaders We Deserve supported McKinney and Valdez. The Working Families Party PAC supported McKinney.

Justice Democrats received $150,000 from Desmos Studio CEO Eli Luberoff and $85,000 from Hims & Hers Health CEO Andrew Dudum.

Android co-founder Rich Miner contributed $65,000 to Leaders We Deserve, while former Google chief scientist Jeff Dean donated $100,000 to the Working Families Party PAC.

Heritage Foundation chief economist E.J. Antoni spelled out for Fox News Digital how executives often support candidates in hopes of securing regulatory "carve-outs, exemptions, and exclusions" if they are elected to positions where they can introduce or influence related policy in the future.

The campaign finance records do not establish that any of the executives sought or received preferential treatment in exchange for their contributions.

Trump Is Desperate For a Ukraine Deal, but the Window Is Closing

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump wants a Ukraine peace deal by early January—before the Democrats, riding high after their stunning midterm election win this month, come sweeping in to take control of Congress.
  • Why exactly does Trump have to get a deal before the upcoming Congress convenes?
  • According to recent reports, the clock is ticking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The clock is ticking. Sources in the White House say U.S. President Donald Trump wants a Ukraine peace deal by early January—before the Democrats, riding high after their stunning midterm election win this month, come sweeping in to take control of Congress. “The Americans are pushing hard and there’s some concern that it would need a great deal of Ukrainian concessions to get anywhere near a deal,” one European official told the Financial Times. “The Americans are in a hurry, Putin is in no hurry,” another said.

But wait—what’s the rush? Why exactly does Trump have to get a deal before the upcoming Congress convenes? Surely he can find plenty of allies in the House and Senate who would be happy to support a just and equitable peace in Ukraine. After all, his goals are purely humanitarian; as he keeps telling us, he just wants to stop the killing.

According to recent reports, the clock is ticking. Sources in the White House say U.S. President Donald Trump wants a Ukraine peace deal by early January—before the Democrats, riding high after their stunning midterm election win this month, come sweeping in to take control of Congress. “The Americans are pushing hard and there’s some concern that it would need a great deal of Ukrainian concessions to get anywhere near a deal,” one European official told the Financial Times. “The Americans are in a hurry, Putin is in no hurry,” another stated.

According to recent reports, but wait—what’s the rush? Why exactly does Trump have to get a deal before the new Congress convenes? Surely he can find plenty of allies in the House and Senate who would be happy to support a just and equitable peace in Ukraine. After all, his goals are purely humanitarian; as he keeps telling us, he just wants to stop the killing.

If saving lives were really his priority, there are plenty of things that Trump could have done by now to achieve that end. He could have increased humanitarian and financial aid to the Ukrainian government. Along with other weapons to bolster Kyiv’s defenses, he could have sent Patriot missiles to protect Ukrainian civilians from ballistic missile attacks, which Russia has been steadily ramping up in recent months. And, even more importantly, he could have pressured Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, rather than gutting sanctions passed by Congress and allowing Moscow to sell diesel fuel on global markets (which hasn’t helped U.S. consumers but has given Russia more funding for its war).

In a recent development, “The United States government is actually trying to get a very good deal for Russia,” as military historian Phillips O’Brien recently told a Ukrainian newspaper. “That’s its starting point.” He dismisses Trump’s professed humanitarian concern, arguing that Trump’s ideological affinity for Putin-style authoritarianism and persistent contempt for Kyiv are driving him to accommodate Russia’s interests while treating the Ukrainians as an afterthought.

The urgency with which Trump is pursuing this agenda also has a tangible financial component. He thinks that Russia is a potential gold mine, and he wants to wet his beak. The Kremlin understands this perfectly well, and the Russians have been working hard to service his expectations. Indeed, the list of potential business deals Moscow is offering Team Trump seems to be growing by the day. Putin has tasked Kirill Dmitriev, the head of Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, to pitch tempting proposals to Trump’s negotiating team, led by son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate tycoon Steve Witkoff. The deals on offer include oil and gas investments and sales of aluminum and critical minerals; many of them would require the lifting of current Western sanctions before funding can flow, a huge incentive for Putin. Dmitriev has claimed that the total value of the projects under discussion amounts to $14 trillion—wildly fanciful but just what Trump wants to hear.

It has been revealed that trump and his cronies stand to benefit personally from these deals. A Texas financier named Gentry Beach, who has close ties to the Trump family, has already signed an agreement with Russian natural gas manufacturer Novatek. Dmitriev has suggested that Elon Musk’s Boring Co. could take part in a project for a tunnel underneath the Bering Strait; it’s a nonsensical notion but demonstrates just how deftly the Kremlin knows how to cater to the Trump World mindset. Trump, of course, wants a cut of his own. In October, the New York Times reported that one of the multibillion-dollar oil deals under discussion with Russia would benefit Middle Eastern investors with links to Kushner and Witkoff. And these are only the projects that we know about.

According to recent reports, hence the need for speed. Trump is clearly hoping that a peace deal will continue to yield dividends to himself and his friends long after he leaves office. Noted differently, the White House is holding a fire sale of U.S. foreign policy to the highest and most likely bidder, which in Trump’s eyes is Putin. In that sense, Trump’s Ukraine policy is merely an extension of his broader program of replacing the U.S. national interest with his own—what the Atlantic’s Anne Applebaum has aptly called an “empire of grift.”.

In a recent development, A post on Trump’s Truth Social account on Nov. 19.Donald Trump/Truth Social.

But first, he has to get a deal signed, and that is looking less likely by the day. The president’s much-ballyhooed trilateral summit in Shenzhen, which was supposed to make Trump look like a global titan, ended without any sort of palpable progress on the Ukrainian front. The terse final communique didn’t mention either Iran or Ukraine (although it did offer up a vague swipe at the International Criminal Court). Neither Chinese President Xi Jinping nor his vassal Putin seems to have regarded the war in Ukraine as worth mentioning.

Sources indicate that that has left Trump, the man who repeatedly claimed that he’d stop the war within 24 hours of taking office, sounding increasingly desperate. On his way back from the summit in China, he assured European leaders that the Kremlin was keen on peace: “Putin wants to end the war. He wants the deal done. He is getting tired of this.” Shortly thereafter, Putin demonstrated his peace-loving credentials by raining missiles down on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown, killing a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic and wounding 52.

It has been revealed that as that example shows, Putin has yet to show that he’s actually interested in peace on any but maximalist terms. The Russian leader thinks he’s winning and that all he has to do is stay the course. In October, the Russians launched a record 153 ballistic missiles and 4,000 jet-powered attack drones into Ukraine. Rather than softening his negotiating position, Putin—encouraged by Trump’s permissiveness—has actually expanded his list of conditions for peace to include completely revising the current European security framework, including a rollback of NATO to its 1997 state. When Kushner recently claimed that Russia wouldn’t oppose Western security guarantees for Kyiv, a Putin aide immediately slapped him down.

Sources indicate that it’s not just a failure of tactics. It’s an entirely mistaken worldview.

Three diminished leaders produced symbolism without substance, but their ideological alignment is historic.

Whether Putin actually knows how bad things are or bases his intransigence on rosy assessments from advisors is hard to say. But the Ukrainians aren’t letting up. Keen to demonstrate that the great powers can’t afford to exclude it, Kyiv prefaced the Shenzhen summit with a stunningly effective attack on the Kerch Bridge, a crucial lifeline connecting Russian-occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. That was a carefully calculated middle finger aimed at Putin, who has turned the bridge into a symbol of Crimea’s allegedly indelible link with Russia.

Industry observers note that there was a message for the Americans folded into that attack as well. In recent months, the Ukrainians have been experiencing slowdowns in their access to Starlink and Starshield, the Musk-owned satellite networks that Kyiv has used throughout the war to target Russian positions. Neither Musk nor the White House has been willing to admit responsibility for the lags, but many in Kyiv see the restrictions as a form of tacit U.S. pressure to comply with any deal the White House deems acceptable. (There are also rumors that Russia has threatened to attack the satellites.) So the Ukrainians decided to send a signal of their own—by attacking the bridge, one of Moscow’s most heavily protected assets, without using Starlink at all. The military planners in Kyiv came up with an entirely indigenous solution to the problem.

In a recent development, this isn’t the only way that the Ukrainians have been showing that they still have cards to play (to use the phrase wielded by Trump in his notorious Oval Office bullying of Zelensky). Ukraine has effectively stymied Russian efforts to capture territory this year; Russia actually lost ground in September and October, not least thanks to daring Ukrainian offensive operations incorporating remotely controlled ground vehicles. Ukraine’s General Staff claims that the Russians incurred 54,400 casualties (killed, wounded, or missing) in October alone, which would make it the bloodiest month of the war. When Trump urged the Ukrainians to cease their attacks on Russian oil refineries, they simply ignored him. Those strikes are one of their most effective ways of inflicting pain on the enemy, and they’re in no mood to capitulate.

According to recent reports, trump’s efforts to engineer peace are also running up against the stubbornness of the Europeans, who for all their dysfunction aren’t ready to give up. Given all these adverse conditions, it’s hard to imagine how the president and his feckless negotiating team will be able to get their way before the new crop of Democrats moves into Congress. But you never know. As a great American philosopher once said: “It ain’t over till it’s over.”.

Attorney General Todd Blanche argues that President Donald Trump evaded prison time by winning the 2024 presidential election on 'Hang Out with Sean Hannity.'.

A federal appeals court handed President Donald Trump a legal victory Monday, reviving his bid to wrest his Newly introduced York hush money case from state court and potentially overturn his felony conviction on presidential immunity grounds.

The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that an August decision by the late U. S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, a Clinton appointee who died in October, that denied Trump's second transfer bid was improper.

The criminal case centered on Trump's reimbursement of his then-attorney Michael Cohen, who paid adult film actress Stormy Daniels $130,000 shortly before the 2016 election to keep her from publicizing an alleged sexual encounter with Trump a decade earlier.

Trump, who denies the encounter, was found guilty in May 2024 of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records.

FEDERAL APPEALS COURT REFUSES TO REHEAR TRUMP APPEAL OF $83M E JEAN CARROLL DEFAMATION JUDGMENT.

At his January 2025 sentencing — days before his second inauguration — Trump received an unconditional discharge, leaving him with no prison time or fine, though the felony conviction remains on his record.

Trump has continued fighting to move the case out of state court, scoring a victory before a three-judge appellate panel Monday.

Recent findings suggest that todd Blanche, former personal attorney for former U.S. President Donald Trump; Trump; and Emil Bove, attorney for Trump, appear in Manhattan criminal court in Fresh York May 29, 2024. (Doug Mills/The New York Times/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

According to recent reports, "We disagree with the district court," said circuit judges Raymond J. Lohier Jr., an Obama appointee; José A. Cabranes, a Clinton appointee; and John M. Walker Jr., a George H. W. Bush appointee.

The panel found Hellerstein made two legal errors: A federal official can still seek removal after being convicted, and Trump showed "good cause" to file a second removal notice. A full written opinion will follow "in due course," the judges wrote.

Trump's attorneys argued in a September brief that the legal landscape had fundamentally changed since his first attempt to transfer the case in 2023. They pointed to the Supreme Court's July 2024 immunity decision, arguing that Manhattan prosecutors had relied on evidence of Trump's presidential activities at trial that the high court subsequently deemed off-limits.

Trump attorney Robert Giuffra Jr. warned that leaving the case in New York's judicial system could significantly delay the president's ability to seek relief from the nation's highest court, arguing Trump "will likely have to wait years.".

TRUMP'S LAWYERS PUT DEM AG ON NOTICE FOR TARGETING HIS FAMILY IN NY FRAUD FIGHT: 'CANNOT STAND'.

Michael Cohen on May 20, 2024, in New York City (Andrea Renault/Star Max/GC Images).

Manhattan prosecutors had urged the 2nd Circuit to uphold Hellerstein's denial, arguing Trump engaged in "strategic delay" by testing his immunity claim in state court first and seeking a transfer only when he believed he would lose. They also maintained that falsifying business records over a personal payoff had nothing to do with official duties.

The ruling puts the question of federal jurisdiction before U.S. District Judge Lewis J. Liman, who inherited the case after Hellerstein's death. The appellate panel also requested that New York courts suspend further proceedings while the jurisdiction dispute is resolved.

President Donald Trump appeared in Manhattan Criminal Court with attorneys Todd Blanche and Emil Bove May 16, 2024, in New York City, during his trial on charges related to alleged hush money payments. (Victor J. Blue-Pool/Getty Images).

If Liman grants the transfer, the federal court will adopt the conviction, setting up a clash over whether it must be vacated under the Supreme Court's immunity standard. Moving the case would not allow Trump to pardon himself, however, because the underlying charges remain New York state offenses outside the reach of a presidential pardon.

#169739. Breaking: Why Israel Is Losing America

Breaking: Why Israel Is Losing America

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, ANDREW P.
  • Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Important Ally.
  • American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ANDREW P. MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress. He was Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Israeli-Palestinian Affairs in the Biden administration and Director for Egypt and Israel Military Concerns on the National Security Council in the Obama administration.

Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Important Ally.

American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

In a recent development, as I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

According to recent reports, things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a new paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

This change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

Whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a upcoming U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

In a recent development, trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

Time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace plan for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is currently marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

Moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he mentioned himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

Trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

It has been revealed that trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

Industry observers note that unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising new ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

In a recent development, israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, confirmed wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

Industry observers note that israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

Recent findings suggest that without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

It is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

Israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with new realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s blueprint for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

It has been revealed that israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

Sources indicate that israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of fresh Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

Israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

It has been revealed that these steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

Recent findings suggest that if Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Without access to international markets and capital, its economy, which has withstood the turmoil of the last several years remarkably well, will suffer and living standards will fall. Under these circumstances, Jewish Israeli citizens with second passports may elect to leave, depriving the state of its raison d’être—providing a safe and prosperous homeland for the Jewish people. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.
