Can Shenzhen Summit Reduce Nuclear Risk?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the recent summit between U.S.
  • The expiration of Fresh START, a 2011 treaty that built on past arms control efforts, in February left the United States and Russia without legally binding limits on their deployed strategic nuclear forces.
  • President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping promised to “conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.” But what that means is unclear, especially when arms control itself has become a politically fraught term across multiple spheres.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

According to recent reports, the recent summit between U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping promised to “conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.” But what that means is unclear, especially when arms control itself has become a politically fraught term across multiple spheres.

The expiration of Fresh START, a 2011 treaty that built on past arms control efforts, in February left the United States and Russia without legally binding limits on their deployed strategic nuclear forces. Some North Korea watchers worry that arms control negotiations would mean abandoning denuclearization as a policy objective, even though interim measures could contribute to the longer-term goal. Meanwhile, China has long resisted trilateral arms control talks, citing the disparity between its arsenal and those of the United States and Russia.

The recent summit between U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping promised to “conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.” But what that means is unclear, especially when arms control itself has become a politically fraught term across multiple spheres.

It has been revealed that the expiration of New START, a 2011 treaty that built on past arms control efforts, in February left the United States and Russia without legally binding limits on their deployed strategic nuclear forces. Some North Korea watchers worry that arms control negotiations would mean abandoning denuclearization as a policy objective, even though interim measures could contribute to the longer-term goal. Meanwhile, China has long resisted trilateral arms control talks, citing the disparity between its arsenal and those of the United States and Russia.

The Shenzen trilateral declaration nevertheless represents a modest but potentially meaningful diplomatic opening. China’s willingness to discuss nuclear dangers is noteworthy given its resistance to negotiations on nuclear arms limitations. However, the declaration provides no timetable, no delegation, and no agreement on specific measures. It remains an open question whether the three countries can translate that commitment into practical cooperation.

Arms control does not have to begin with a treaty. Arms control and nuclear risk reduction are distinct but overlapping approaches to managing nuclear competition, reducing the dangers of miscalculation, and building confidence among adversaries. Measures such as missile launch notifications and crisis communications can be pursued independently of a formal arms control treaty.

Sources indicate that A trilateral arms control treaty remains a distant prospect because of China’s reluctance and Moscow’s demands for changes in broader U.S. policy regarding military support for Ukraine and NATO’s role in European security, and its insistence that multilateral arms control negotiations include the nuclear forces of the United Kingdom and France. But Washington, Beijing, and Moscow do not need to wait for a treaty before taking steps to reduce nuclear risks.

Sources indicate that two days before the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, I suggested at the Track 1.5 Stockholm China Forum that a positive outcome of a Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would be if they reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought (also known as the 1985 Reagan-Gorbachev principle) and that they should begin talks on nuclear risk reduction. That was the language the leaders agreed to in Shenzhen.

In a recent development, however, neither the principle nor the idea of risk reduction talks is latest. In 2022, the P5—the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States)—had reaffirmed the same principle. Reaffirming it again was easier than agreeing on concrete measures that reduce nuclear dangers.

Sources indicate that at least three obstacles could undermine the Shenzhen declaration: geopolitical crises, disagreements over the sources of nuclear risk and their appropriate measures, and incompatible conditions in other areas for progress on risk reduction. Take geopolitical tensions first. Beijing could suspend talks with Washington because of a confrontation over Taiwan or tensions from U.S. arms sales or military activities. A prolonged war in Ukraine and disagreements over European security could also hinder sustained dialogue and cooperation. The trilateral format creates an additional vulnerability: a crisis between any two participants could jeopardize the dialogue even if the third party wants to continue it.

The three countries may also disagree on what constitutes nuclear risk reduction and how best to achieve it. Beijing has tended to emphasize U.S. policies and military capabilities that it considers to be key sources of nuclear risk while Washington has placed greater emphasis on operational measures like establishing crisis hotlines to prevent misunderstanding, miscalculation, and unintended escalation.

In a recent development, therefore, China might favor a discussion on strategic intentions, nuclear doctrines, or mutual no-first-use commitments while Washington would likely prioritize concrete measures such as missile launch notifications, reliable crisis communications, and greater transparency. These approaches are not mutually exclusive, but they reflect different assessments of what makes nuclear conflict more likely and how to manage those risks.

Some risk reduction measures require greater transparency, which China has historically rejected. Meaningful first steps in a risk reduction dialogue would be to provide advance notice of each other’s ballistic missile releases and create a crisis communications channel. However, Washington and Beijing currently do not practice advance notifications in the way that Washington and Moscow or Beijing and Moscow do.

China’s submarine-debuted ballistic missile test in July illustrates the problem. While Beijing said that it notified relevant countries in advance, the notification fell short of the 24-hour standard urged by the United States and other countries.

Washington has already proposed this year that the P5 work on ballistic missile launch notifications and establish a P5 secure communications network, but it had “not yet gained consensus.” Therefore, the Shenzhen declaration raises the question of whether the three largest nuclear powers can make progress on proposals that have encountered resistance in the broader P5 process.

As for crisis communications, the challenge is not simply establishing a direct link between Washington and Beijing. Some channels already exist, but their effectiveness depends on whether urgent messages reach the appropriate decision-makers and receive timely responses. Existing models include the Washington-Moscow Direct Communications Link, which was established in 1963 at the leadership level after the Cuban missile crisis, and the Nuclear Risk Reduction Centers, which were established in 1987 to facilitate routine notifications and messages under arms control and risk reduction arrangements.

A similar arrangement simply does not exist between the United States and China. The limitations of existing channels became apparent in February 2023, when Beijing refused to answer a call from U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin, who was using a defense phone line established in 2008, to explain the U.S. shootdown of a Chinese surveillance balloon and ease tensions. The establishment of an institutionalized channel would require agreed procedures, designated authorities, and a commitment to maintain reliable communications even during periods of heightened tension.

Industry observers note that progress could also stall if governments make nuclear risk reduction conditional on concessions in other disputes. Beijing could seek changes in U.S. policy toward Taiwan or missile defense, while Moscow could press Washington on broader bilateral relations or on French and British nuclear forces. Such demands could hold nuclear risk reduction hostage to broader geopolitical disagreements.

Despite these obstacles, all three countries have an interest in reducing nuclear dangers. An initial trilateral dialogue could accommodate their competing priorities without requiring the three nuclear powers to agree on the exact causes of strategic instability.

Recent findings suggest that they could begin by exchanging views on strategic intentions, nuclear doctrines, and behaviors that each considers destabilizing, while simultaneously exploring practical measures including missile launch notifications and crisis communications. They could also examine how the integration of artificial intelligence into military and nuclear-related systems might introduce upcoming risks and what safeguards could help mitigate them. The immediate goal would be to identify risks that all three governments have an interest in reducing, even if they disagree on their origins.

According to recent reports, the implications of nuclear risk reduction and prospects for eventual arms control extend beyond the United States, China, and Russia. U.S. allies are watching how Washington manages nuclear competition with Beijing and Moscow, how it responds to North Korea’s advancing nuclear capabilities, and how it maintains the credibility of its security commitments. The Shenzhen declaration’s silence on North Korea’s nuclear program raises questions about how the three nuclear powers intend to reconcile their commitment in preventing nuclear proliferation with the security concerns of the United States’ Asian allies.

Industry observers note that the United States will need to negotiate measures with its two nuclear competitors in ways that reduce the risk of great-power conflict without weakening regional deterrence or creating new incentives for nuclear proliferation. But that requires more than a trilateral treaty. Washington will need to consider how its allies assess the implications of any future trilateral agreement for their own security, rather than treating their concerns as secondary to great-power negotiations.

Duyeon Kim is a research fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies and a long-time foreign-policy and national security expert who has held senior positions at leading Washington, D.C. think tanks.

#169735. Tech Report: The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

Tech Report: The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.
  • According to recent reports, since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested.
  • Sources indicate that turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.

Ankara’s Risky Bid to Impose Regional Order.

According to recent reports, since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested. The previous Gulf-centered order had Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) trying to stabilize and shape the region using economic statecraft and the normalization of relations with former foes in Iran, Israel, Turkey, and Syria. Three years of war in Gaza, and more recently in Iran and the Gulf, have severely disrupted that order-building project and generated a deep sense of uncertainty about what comes next.

Sources indicate that turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum. Before 2023, Ankara’s influence had been in decline; after years of diplomatic isolation following the Arab uprisings, it had just begun repairing its ties with major regional actors. But in the past few years, Turkey has earned American backing for its policies in Syria and its regional diplomacy, and it has made an effort to secure the home front by pursuing a peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), a militant group that has fought a decades-long insurgency against the Turkish state. Most recently, in August, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey signed the Mecca Defense Alliance, a collective security agreement that institutionalizes Turkey’s regional positioning and pulls the country directly into Saudi Arabia’s war with the Houthis.

According to recent reports, turkey’s post–October 7 strategy has restored the country’s position as a regional heavyweight. But it is not capable of meeting its larger objective: establishing order on its own terms. Turkey, like the region’s other aspiring leaders, lacks the power to impose a new security framework on its own. Its nascent efforts to build one, such as the new Mecca pact, merely make countries outside the bloc feel unsafe, feeding instability. Turkey’s most ambitious plays for regional leadership are therefore likely to prove ineffective or even counterproductive. As long as the Middle East’s highly militarized, zero-sum security dynamics remain, Ankara would be better off concentrating on interests closer to home that it has the power to protect.

This is not the first time that Turkey has tried to shape the broader Middle Eastern order. Ankara saw the Arab uprisings in the early 2010s as a historic window of opportunity. The ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) described the political transformation sweeping the region as “the people’s coming to power,” and the Turkish government expected that eventual elections in the Arab countries rocked by protest would bring into office parties aligned with the Muslim Brotherhood, which was ideologically sympathetic and had practical links to the AKP. The emergence of friendly governments, the thinking went, would increase Turkey’s influence in the region.

Yet these hopes soon receded. Egypt’s Muslim Brotherhood–affiliated president, Mohamed Morsi, was overthrown in 2013, and Turkey’s bet on the opposition movement in Syria failed as Bashar al-Assad clung to power. Turkey was left isolated. A rival axis composed of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE objected to Turkey’s Muslim Brotherhood ties and sought to limit Ankara’s influence. This group contested Turkey’s positions across the Middle East, North Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, and the Horn of Africa, effectively fighting proxy battles with Turkey in conflicts in Libya, Somalia, and Syria.

Industry observers note that then, the attacks on October 7, 2023, ushered in another period of upheaval. Some changes since have played in Turkey’s favor. Chief among them is the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024 at the hands of opposition groups led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham. Turkey had arguably invested more than any other country in pursuit of regime change in Damascus; it assisted opposition groups for years. Yet as the years went by, that objective seemed increasingly out of reach. The region’s other major powers made their peace with the regime’s survival, and even Ankara began considering rapprochement with Assad to avoid being left out in the cold. Assad’s fall changed Turkey’s fortunes overnight, handing it a level of influence in Syria it had not held in more than a decade.

It has been revealed that other developments proved more dangerous for Ankara. Israel’s foreign policy became more assertive and revisionist after October 7, and its expansive security objectives began to clash with Turkey’s own. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s sharp criticism of Israeli policies in Gaza strained the relationship, and it deteriorated further when Turkey expanded its foothold in post-Assad Syria and Israel came to view Ankara’s military presence there as a direct threat. As Israel continues to strike sites in Syria—attacks Ankara has condemned—the risk of escalation is only growing. A miscalculation on either side could lead to a direct clash between Israeli and Turkish forces.

Sources indicate that the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, meanwhile, has cut both ways for Turkey. While Tehran’s attention has been focused elsewhere, Ankara has welcomed Iran’s retreat from Syria and the chance to push back against its remaining influence in Iraq. Turkey also has no interest in seeing a nuclear-armed Iran upend the regional balance of power. Yet the prospect of chaos across Turkey’s eastern border, should the Iranian regime fall, has bred real anxiety in Ankara, as has the possibility that Iran could become emboldened if the regime emerges from the war intact.

In this complex environment, Ankara has pursued a three-pronged strategy to protect its security interests and, it hopes, capitalize on opportunities the upheaval has created. Since U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to power, Erdogan has drawn Turkey closer to the United States and tried to use his relationship with Washington to advance Ankara’s regional policies. Turkey has also pressed ahead with regional normalization, building on efforts to repair ties with Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other key Arab countries in the early 2020s, with the aim to forge a broader regional bloc. And, domestically, Ankara launched the “Turkey Without Terror” process, an attempt to resolve the conflict with the PKK inside and outside Turkey, which Turkey’s adversaries have long exploited by arming Kurdish groups or backing them politically.

Some of Ankara’s policies have borne fruit. Consider, for instance, the outreach to Washington. Erdogan’s close relations with Trump helped bring the United States on board with Turkey’s expanded role in Syria. Turkey was one of the four countries Washington brought in to help negotiate the U.S.-proposed October 2025 cease-fire agreement between Israel and Hamas, and as a result, Trump offered and Erdogan accepted a seat on the U.S. president’s so-called Board of Peace for Gaza’s reconstruction. Turkey has played an active part mediating between the United States and Iran during the latest war. And Trump publicly endorsed the Mecca Defense Alliance, calling it “big, bold, and notable.” All of this points to a recognition in Washington of Turkey’s regional importance, the U.S. administration’s willingness to support some of Ankara’s priorities, and Turkey’s determination to elevate its own position.

It has been revealed that yet there are undeniable limits to Turkey’s quest for influence. At a February 2026 Board of Peace summit, for instance, Turkey was excluded from participating in a planned international troop deployment and police training in Gaza—a sign that warming relations with Washington were not enough to override Israeli objections to having a Turkish military footprint in the Palestinian territory. In Syria, similarly, the support Turkey has secured from the Trump administration has not stopped Israel from launching military strikes at Syrian targets near Turkish positions. Simply put, Turkey has not been able to use its relationship with the Trump administration to overcome the limit Israeli opposition places on the scope of Turkey’s regional role.

In a recent development, turkey’s regional normalization efforts have yielded mixed results, too. Restoring diplomatic ties with significant players such as Saudi Arabia is in Turkey’s interest, to be sure. But the alliances Ankara is entering with these countries risk making Turkey and the region less secure, not more. The Mecca pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia could end up hardening rival blocs and elevating regional tensions. Turkey insists that the alliance is directed against no country in particular and has suggested that Egypt, Syria, or even Iran could eventually join. But in the meantime, Iran, Israel, and the Houthis could see it as a threat and try to test or weaken its members’ commitment.

It has been revealed that furthermore, the pact could pull Turkey into other countries’ wars. That possibility is already on the table now that the Turkish parliament has ratified the agreement and the Houthis are escalating their attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Turkish government has insisted that any military support it provided would be confined to deterrence, intelligence sharing, and defense-industrial cooperation. Yet Saudi Arabia is now seeking Pakistan’s and Turkey’s help with air defense and territorial protection, and the three states have agreed to prepare forces for rapid deployment. Sending Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia would still require separate parliamentary approval. If parliament allowed it, even a limited deployment would risk drawing Turkey into a wider regional conflict.

Sources indicate that some kind of regional security framework is necessary. The problem is that no country in the region, including Turkey, has the power to impose a security order on the rest, so whenever someone tries, other countries feel threatened. An informal cooperation framework that is open to all countries in the region—and that asks its members to commit to nonaggression instead of making mutual-defense pledges—might work better. But the assembly and functioning of such a coalition require trust that governments in the region do not have. Breaking the impasse would likely require the United States to play a more constructive role than it has in recent years—not simply endorsing whatever regional arrangement emerges, as Trump did with the Mecca pact, or pressuring countries to normalize relations with Israel without expecting Israel to change its policies in return, as Trump has also done. Instead, Washington, perhaps with the help of Beijing, would need to compel regional rivals such as Iran and Saudi Arabia to take confidence-building measures that would make an inclusive security framework viable in the long run. Without this external push, the narrower security blocs that emerge in the region will only lead to further instability.

Ankara’s strongest cards lie closer to home. The Kurdish peace process has moved slowly since February 2025, when Abdullah Ocalan, the imprisoned leader of the PKK, called on the militant group to disarm. But it has yielded tangible progress. In May 2025, the PKK declared that it would dissolve. In Syria, Kurdish forces are being integrated into the Syrian army, and Mazloum Abdi, the commander of the People’s Defense Units, a Kurdish armed group affiliated with the PKK, was appointed as a presidential adviser in August. Syria’s postconflict transition remains fragile, and the reconciliation between Damascus and Kurdish militants in the northeast may owe as much to American pressure as it does to Turkey’s domestic efforts to make peace with the PKK. But for Turkey, the eventual integration of Syrian Kurdish forces into the Syrian state removes the risk Ankara saw in having an autonomous, armed Kurdish entity on its southern border. And, given the close security and economic ties Ankara has developed with Damascus, as well as the political and legal steps the government can take at home to complete the disbanding of the PKK and to deepen democratic reforms, Turkey has the ability to keep these encouraging developments on track.

Recent findings suggest that turkey’s regional policies are most successful when the country plays to its strengths—not when it is trying to throw its weight around the region. In the first decade of the twenty-first century, Ankara built real influence by mediating between Syria and Israel and between Palestinian factions, expanding its economic engagement in the Levant, and proposing projects to connect the region’s energy and transportation infrastructure. Military power, meanwhile, has proved most effective when applied for specific purposes, such as to secure the border with Syria. This combination is Turkey’s winning formula: diplomacy and economic outreach to extend its influence, and limited force to protect its core interests. Broad, open-ended commitments, by contrast, risk drawing Turkey into regional conflicts without making it safer.

It has been revealed that today, sticking to a more effective formula does not mean retreating from regional politics. It means setting priorities and planning long-term. Consolidating the Kurdish peace process, keeping Washington invested in Syria’s stabilization, managing the risk of confrontation with Israel in Syria, and maintaining constructive relations with the Kurdistan Regional Government in northern Iraq and the Iraqi government in Baghdad are key to keeping Turkey’s borders secure and are within Turkey’s ability to achieve. Ankara can continue to use its experience in mediation when opportunities to advance peace processes present themselves. It can also promote economic connectivity, both by expanding trade ties and by supporting regional infrastructure projects such as the Iraq-Europe Development Road and a proposed pipeline network connecting the Gulf to Jordan, Syria, and Turkey. It need not shy away from security cooperation with the Gulf, either, if it can engage without making formal commitments. Yet in all these endeavors, Ankara should remember that it has the most clout when it stays out of the region’s conflicts.

According to recent reports, the Middle East’s escalating wars and rival blocs could make a narrower Turkish security policy more difficult to sustain today than it was in the past. Defending Ankara’s interests and playing a constructive role in a volatile neighborhood will require a careful balance. The best way Turkey can contribute to regional stability may be to avoid trying to do too much.

Richard Volpe, professor of agricultural economics at California Polytechnic State University, explains how higher prices for food, energy, packaging and transportation could make holiday meals harder on household budgets.

The turkey may be a holiday bargain, but rising prices for meat, dairy and fresh foods could make the rest of the Thanksgiving spread cost much more this year.

Richard Volpe, a professor of agribusiness at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, told Fox News Digital that sustained high energy costs in the midst of the Iran war — particularly for diesel — are pushing up grocery prices just as households prepare to host holiday meals.

Surging prices of ham and eggnog, in particular, could put a damper on some holiday favorites.

Recent findings suggest that shoppers can compare prices, watch for store promotions and consider store brands to keep holiday grocery bills in check. (Kim Raff/Bloomberg/Getty Images).

"Most of the biggest increases are things like fruits, vegetables and meats," Volpe said. "Fresh and refrigerated foods feel those costs sooner than shelf-stable products.".

7 COSTCO THANKSGIVING FOOD DEALS AND STEALS THAT SHOPPERS CAN'T MISS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON.

Dairy is also especially energy and transportation intensive, putting holiday staples such as butter and eggnog under pressure.

Volpe noted shoppers willing to switch brands and take advantage of store promotions can keep holiday meals more affordable.

"If you are less worried about brand or banner loyalty, and you’re able to follow promotions and look for these sort of aggressive, enticing deals, there are still ways to achieve savings and to keep those Thanksgiving and holiday dinners relatively affordable," Volpe remarked.

Sources indicate that with beef and pork prices high, some households may serve turkey for other holiday meals in place of pot roast or ham. (iStock).

He also acknowledged that high beef and pork prices could contribute to some households deciding to dine on a different main dish for their holiday meals this year.

"Beef and pork are particularly expensive right now, so I would expect to see some substitutions there," he remarked. "I would strongly suspect that across the country, there are folks who are roasting turkeys and chickens, or even salmon or some other large sort of centerpiece to the meal that’s protein-based other than beef and pork.".

AMERICANS ARE MAKING COSTLY GROCERY MISTAKE EVEN BEFORE ENTERING THE STORE, EXPERT WARNS.

Swapping the menu may help, but Volpe mentioned skipping the grocery store for a restaurant or catered meal is unlikely to save money.

"It is still cheaper to go to the grocery store and prepare food at home," Volpe said.

He said restaurant prices have risen nearly twice as fast as grocery prices over the past two to two and a half years.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah makes a notable visit to India, former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina reveals a return date to Bangladesh, and senior Pakistani opposition leaders are detained.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah makes a notable visit to India, former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina announces a return date to Bangladesh, and senior Pakistani opposition leaders are detained.

It has been revealed that nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s two-day visit to Newly introduced Delhi concluded on Monday. Standing alongside Shah, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi revealed a $1.6 billion assistance package for Kathmandu, most of it earmarked for reconstruction after August’s catastrophic floods.

Recent findings suggest that the two sides also pledged cooperation on satellite communications and urban development, and India confirmed that it will open a latest Indian Institute of Technology campus in Nepal. Shah affirmed the strength of the Nepal-India partnership, saying that he hoped it would “be one where trust stands as tall as the Himalayas.”.

According to recent reports, shah, 36, is a highly unconventional leader, known for his love of rapping, dark sunglasses, and video games. After taking office in March, he took a defiant approach to diplomacy, refusing to meet with visiting foreign dignitaries unless they were of similar rank. His unwillingness to meet Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri prompted Upcoming Delhi to call off Misri’s scheduled visit in May.

Recent findings suggest that that Shah made India his first trip abroad as prime minister speaks to the importance of the relationship. It is also a reminder of India’s regional influence at a moment when some commentators argue that India is on the back foot relative to China.

It has been revealed that china has grown increasingly present in Nepal in recent years. In late 2024, the previous Nepali government, led by K.P. Sharma Oli, inked a framework deal with Beijing on the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). Progress has been slow, and Nepal remains one of the only South Asian countries today with no BRI projects on its soil.

It has been revealed that however, Nepal, like other smaller South Asian states, relies heavily on Indian development and humanitarian assistance. This gives Fresh Delhi leverage, even as most regional capitals scale up ties with China.

Sources indicate that the Maldives offers an instructive parallel. One of President Mohamed Muizzu’s first foreign-policy moves after taking office in November 2023 was to expel India’s relatively small military presence. Shortly thereafter, he signed new defense deals with China and signaled a desire to deepen ties further.

Recent findings suggest that yet months later, he visited New Delhi, where Modi unveiled a new financial assistance package at a critical moment of economic distress. In 2024 and 2025, Muizzu repeatedly called India his country’s closest ally.

In a recent development, india is not taking its neighbors for granted, and Shah’s visit showed it. The assistance package was generous, among the largest provided to Nepal since the floods. Modi’s announcement that India will create new innovation hubs and start-up incubators in Nepal will help boost the country’s shaky economy—but it is also likely meant to preempt Beijing from doing the same.

None of this means the relationship is in great shape. India and Nepal face several entrenched challenges entirely unrelated to China, including territorial disputes and public perception problems. Many young Nepalis see India as a bully, a view reinforced by India’s unofficial blockade of Nepal more than a decade ago.

Shah’s visit nevertheless indicates that the two capitals can get substantive things done despite their disagreements, and both walked away with wins. For India, it’s a useful pushback against China. (Shah could, after all, have gone to Beijing first.) For Nepal, it secured badly needed reconstruction aid and pledges of additional economic support, which are hard to come by in a constrained global donor environment.

Hasina reveals return date. Former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who has resided in India since being ousted by mass protests in 2024, indicates she will return home on Dec. 16, her spokesperson told Reuters on Tuesday. The date is symbolic, marking the anniversary of Bangladesh’s 1971 victory over Pakistan.

Recent findings suggest that getting back will not be simple. Hasina was stripped of her passport after her ouster, and Bangladeshi officials have refused to issue a upcoming one. A Bangladeshi court also sentenced her last year to death in absentia for her role in the violent crackdown on protests. Still, Hasina claims she wants to return to challenge the legitimacy of the charges and rally her party, which was banned last year.

Dhaka repeated its standard response: Hasina is a fugitive and cannot return unless India extradites her—something New Delhi, which was close to Hasina during her time in power, is unlikely to do.

Sources indicate that hasina, through her spokesperson, also asked the government to arrange her trip back on Bangladesh’s national carrier, Biman Bangladesh Airlines. Bangladesh’s state minister for foreign affairs called the request “delusional.”.

It has been revealed that if Hasina does return, she will almost certainly be arrested. That would inflame both supporters and opponents, likely sparking violent protests. But if she chooses not to, or tries but is blocked, her base could react violently as well. With major economic, energy, and public health challenges already on its plate, the government can’t afford fresh instability.

Pakistani minister visits India. Pakistan’s climate change minister, Musadik Malik, also traveled to Upcoming Delhi this past week, representing Pakistan at an arts and culture forum organized by the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). It was the first visit by a Pakistani minister since 2023.

It has been revealed that on one level, the visit went as expected. Malik held no bilateral meetings with Indian counterparts, and both governments emphasized that he came in his SCO capacity. With India-Pakistan ties ice cold since last year’s brief but intense conflict, any official bilateral engagement would have been stunning.

What stood out was Malik’s performance. He won admirers in Pakistan, and some in India, with a speech (delivered in Urdu) that emphasized the countries’ shared heritage and praised India’s rich cultural history. He also responded calmly to Indian journalists who peppered him aggressively with questions about Pakistan-sponsored terrorism.

Malik’s trip won’t thaw a frozen bilateral relationship, but it underscored the potential for people-to-people engagement.

It has been revealed that sri Lankan oil spill. Authorities in Sri Lanka moved promptly to respond to an oil leak at Colombo’s main port on Nov. 21, which the Marine Environment Protection Authority stated occurred when a pipeline connected to a fuel storage tank ruptured unexpectedly.

The spill polluted nearly two miles of coastline, including the city’s main drainage canal, a fisheries harbor, and an area where local fishers dock their boats. Fortunately, the port authority stopped most of the leak within an hour. It is unclear how much oil escaped, but the tank reportedly held about 1,000 metric tons of marine gas oil.

It has been revealed that this is the second such incident at the port in under a year. In December 2025, a pipeline sprang a leak while crude oil was being unloaded from a nearby tanker.

Industry observers note that for more than a week, one of Pakistan’s most prominent opposition leaders has been detained, with no details released about his condition or location. All that is known is that on Nov. 17, Taimur Jhagra and two other senior leaders of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party were taken into custody in Peshawar.

The three were already facing legal trouble: The government links them to attacks on a state radio facility in May 2023, though their lawyers say there is no evidence tying them to violence.

Jhagra served as finance and health minister in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province when Imran Khan was prime minister. He oversaw a series of notable health reforms, including the introduction of a universal health insurance program. Many Pakistanis—and not just PTI supporters—view him as thoughtful, clean, and committed to public service.

His arrest, the information blackout that followed, and the lack of a widespread public outcry illustrate the extent of state repression in Pakistan today.

Human rights activist Glenfrey De Mel, writing in the Daily Mirror, praises Sri Lanka’s fresh anti-terrorism legislation: The proposed Anti-Terrorism Act “represents a critical juncture in the nation’s pursuit of a framework that effectively addresses extremist threats while upholding the fundamental pillars of human rights and the rule of law.”.

Industry observers note that student Taiba Akhter Mim warns in the Daily Star of the dangers of Bangladeshi children spending too much time on their devices: “Short, supervised viewing of age-appropriate material is unlikely to ruin a child. What should concern us is endless autoplay. … Before pressing play, we should ask what the video gives a child besides a reason to keep watching.”.

Writer Akbar N. Shad explains in the Express Tribune why Pakistani society holds back from protests: “Pakistan’s political and institutional landscape has, at times, made dissent a difficult undertaking. Concerns about pressure, restrictions and the personal cost of challenging authority can discourage ordinary citizens from raising their voices.”.

Latest Update: Rep. Jimmy Gomez to resign after sexual misconduct probe

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., will resign effective Dec.
  • Gomez, who was defeated in his bid for reelection this month, announced his resignation Monday, hours after the Ethics panel released its final report which also noted Gomez’s conduct “could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., pictured leaving the Capitol on Nov. 9, will resign Dec. 1. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Sources indicate that rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., will resign effective Dec. 1 after the House Ethics Committee remarked it found “substantial evidence” that Gomez engaged in sexual misconduct with a congressional staffer.

Gomez, who was defeated in his bid for reelection this month, announced his resignation Monday, hours after the Ethics panel released its final report which also noted Gomez’s conduct “could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”.

Sources indicate that the report was one of four released by the Ethics panel Monday. Three of them are about members who are set to depart the House after the 119th Congress, and the fourth is about the conduct of a former chief of staff.

In a statement, Gomez said he took “full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage,” but that he also had “strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions.” Despite his concerns with the process, though, he said he saw no alternative other than to resign because “he was not given an opportunity to respond” to the final report.

A statement issued by lawyers representing the female staffer with whom Gomez was accused of engaging in misconduct applauded the “thorough and sensitive” handling of the investigation.

“However, Representative Gomez’s conduct did not occur in a vacuum, and immediate steps must be taken by Congress to rein in what the report describes as a ‘toxic and predatory culture,’” the attorneys, Lisa J. Banks and Sarah E. Nesbitt, added. “Democracy cannot function properly when women must endure harassment and abuse as a condition of public service.”.

The committee began investigating Gomez after a New York Post story alleged the congressman was seen kissing a congressional staffer at a party hosted by then-Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif. At the time, Gomez said he did not violate any House ethics rules. Swalwell resigned earlier this year amid a slew of sexual assault allegations from four separate women, one of whom was a former staffer.

But the more serious allegations addressed by the Ethics probe involve another female staffer, identified in the report as Witness 1. She testified in a deposition with the committee that on one occasion, Gomez touched her genitals without consent at a Washington bar. Gomez remarked in his own interview with the committee that while he did engage in sexual conduct with the staffer, “she did not say no, she did not push me away.”.

The same staffer, who did not work for Gomez, noted he made inappropriate advances in a separate incident in Gomez’s congressional office, which Gomez downplayed as just a “beso,” or kiss, and hug.

In its report, the committee determined that the congressional staffer’s testimony “was clear and was supported by evidence that she contemporaneously complained of his conduct” to another witness, and was part of an intolerable “toxic and predatory culture” on Capitol Hill.

A statement issued by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and other House Democratic leaders called the report “serious and deeply troubling,” and that Gomez’s resignation was “appropriate.”.

“Decisive action to set a upcoming standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats,” the statement noted.

Gomez was one of two House members from the Golden State to lose to a fellow Democrat earlier this month. Northern California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones.

Gomez faced off against Angela Gonzales-Torres in the general election after both advanced from the state’s all-party primary in June. Gonzales-Torres, a Democratic Socialist and housing advocate, had the backing of several progressive groups, including Justice Democrats and Leaders We Deserve. Her supporters criticized Gomez after the House Ethics panel opened its investigation in August. Her campaign also sought to publicize the inquiry in the weeks leading up to Election Day, The Washington Post reported.

The committee also released findings of its probes into Reps. Mike Collins, R-Ga., and Troy Nehls, R-Texas, as well as Brandon Phillips, Collins’ former chief of staff.

Collins, who lost his Senate bid earlier this month, was under review following an Office of Congressional Conduct referral alleging that Phillips hired his girlfriend as an intern. Collins’ lawyers denied the allegations, and Phillips was fired earlier this year.

According to recent reports, collins and the committee reached a mutual agreement under which he would return $2,880 to the U.S. Treasury after the committee found he had overpaid the “intern,” allowing it to close the case.

Phillips, who did not comply with his congressional subpoenas, has been recommended by the committee to be held in contempt of Congress.

It has been revealed that “At no point did Mr. Phillips offer a satisfactory legal justification for his failure to comply with the subpoena,” the committee wrote.

Sources indicate that the committee probed Nehls for allegedly using campaign money for his personal benefit. Nehls did not run for reelection, but his twin brother, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, will replace him in January.

The committee found that the Texas Republican “improperly used a company that he owned as a political committee; the company, Liberty 1776, received and disbursed funds for the benefit of Representative Nehls’ campaign and other unverifiable purposes.”.

Daniela Altimari contributed to this report.

In a recent development, senator John Fetterman joins 'Saturday in America' for his first interview since the midterms. Fetterman discusses the rise of far-left candidates in the Democratic Party, potential investigations and facing primary challenges.

Industry observers note that donald Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points in 2024. Two years later, Democrat Scott Colom won the state’s Senate race, ending a Republican hold that had lasted more than four decades.

Sources indicate that colom’s victory was part of a string of Democratic breakthroughs during the midterms in places Trump had carried by double digits. Democrats also won Senate races in Kansas and South Carolina, captured the Texas governor’s office and flipped a Republican-held House seat deep in Trump country in Indiana that had not elected a Democrat since 1990.

The results stand out for more than the presidential margins as well — Democrats broke Senate streaks that had lasted decades and defeated Republican incumbents in races many expected the GOP to hold, including one where the Democratic challenger spent next to nothing on television advertisements.

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE.

Here are five of the year’s most striking upsets:.

Democratic and Republican Party emblems are displayed with an American flag background in this photo illustration taken on Aug. 25, 2022. Democrats flipped several red-state seats during the 2026 midterm elections. (Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images).

Trump carried the state by nearly 23 points in 2024, and a Democrat had not won a U.S. Senate race in Mississippi since 1982. Several major election forecasters rated the contest Solid Republican for much of the cycle, before shifting it to Likely Republican as the race tightened.

It has been revealed that colom, a district attorney, defeated Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., by less than one percentage point, 49.36% to 48.54%, according to Associated Press election results. Hyde-Smith had Trump’s backing, and the president rallied for her in the campaign’s final days. Meanwhile, the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, made a seven-figure late-campaign ad buy, as previously reported by Fox News Digital.

The Associated Press did not call the race until Nov. 11, more than a week after Election Day. Colom will also become the first Black senator to represent Mississippi since Reconstruction.

Sources indicate that the margin was razor-thin, but the political barrier was enormous — a Trump +23 state, a Trump-backed incumbent and a 44-year drought in Democratic Senate victories. But Democrats pulled off the upset.

Sources indicate that scott Colom walks across the campus of Jackson State University on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026, in Jackson, Miss. Colom defeated Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, ending a 44-year Democratic Senate drought in the state. (Aron Smith/Jackson State University via Getty Images).

Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative, defeated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, R-Texas, as he sought an unprecedented fourth term, ending a 36-year Democratic losing streak in Texas governor’s races. Trump had carried the state by 13.7 points in 2024, according to Associated Press election data, and an October Fox News poll demonstrated Abbott ahead leading up to the Nov. 3 election. Hinojosa, however, ultimately won with 52.8% of the vote to Abbott’s 45.7%, according to Associated Press election results.

Her victory was a major break from Texas’ recent political history and a miss by many major polls. It also made Hinojosa the state’s first Latina governor. Democrats had not won the governor’s office since Ann Richards’ 1990 victory.

Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa speaks during a campaign rally in Austin on Nov. 2, 2026. She unseated GOP Gov. Greg Abbott. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

Hinojosa’s win was one of two Democratic statewide breakthroughs in Texas, as Democratic state Rep. James Talarico also defeated Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Senate race.

CHUCK DEVORE: TEXAS TURNS BLUE, BUT HERE’S WHERE THE NEXT 4 BIG BATTLES ARE COMING.

South Carolina had not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1998, when Fritz Hollings won his final term, and Trump carried the state by nearly 18 points in 2024, according to Associated Press election data. Andrews, a Democratic pediatrician who had never held elected office before, defeated appointed Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, by nearly five points.

Recent findings suggest that graham had Trump’s endorsement and the president also helped her with late campaign appearances on the trail. She had been appointed to serve out her brother’s term after his death, then won the Republican nomination for a full six-year term.

Andrews’ win broke a nearly three-decade Republican hold on the state’s Senate seat and became a rare moment when a Trump-backed candidate lost in a state Republicans had long counted on.

Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews face off during a South Carolina U.S. Senate debate in Columbia on Oct. 11, 2026. Andrews went on to defeat Graham, ending a nearly three-decade Republican hold on the seat. (Courtesy: SCETV).

Kansas had not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932, when George McGill won a full term. Hamilton, a Democrat and the founding pastor of a large United Methodist church, defeated first-term Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in a state Trump carried by 16 points in 2024, according to election data from the Associated Press.

The Kansas race was long viewed as a Republican hold, but major election forecasters moved it into toss-up territory late in the campaign as Marshall faced scrutiny over his residency and lawsuits his former medical practice filed against patients.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance both campaigned for Marshall, and Republican-aligned groups spent heavily to keep the seat, including more than $26 million committed to ads supporting him after the August primary — more than was spent on Marshall during his first race in 2020, according to AdImpact data cited by the Associated Press.

Hamilton’s win ended a 94-year Republican Senate streak.

According to recent reports, sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., left, and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, who became the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932. (Getty Images).

Democrat J.D. Ford defeated three-term Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-Ind., in Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, which Trump carried by about 17 points, according to Associated Press election results from 2024. Spartz had won re-election there by 18.6 points in 2024, and the district had not elected a Democrat since 1990, when Jim Jontz won.

It has been revealed that ford, a Democratic state senator, won 51.7% to Spartz’s 48.3%, according to the Associated Press results after the midterms. His victory was the only Indiana House seat to change parties, making it a sharp reversal in a state that Trump carried by 19 points statewide in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that democrats also flipped several other Republican-held House seats in districts Trump carried by double digits, including in North Carolina. Democrat Richard Ojeda defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, R-N.C., who chaired the National Republican Congressional Committee, the House GOP’s campaign and fundraising arm. Hudson was charged with helping protect the Republican majority, and he had raised $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million and won the district by nearly 19 points in 2024, while Trump had carried it by 16 points.

According to recent reports, in North Carolina’s 6th District, Democrat Cyril Jefferson defeated first-term Rep. Addison McDowell, R-N.C., in a district Trump carried by nearly 17 points, and Democrat Zach Dembo also flipped an open, Republican-held seat in Kentucky’s 6th District, beating Republican Ralph Alvarado by 9.4 points in a district Trump had carried by roughly 15 points in 2024.

In a recent development, meanwhile, a razor-thin margin in Tennessee’s 4th District underscores the challenges Republicans faced across several traditionally safe districts. Democrat Victoria Broderick, who spent under $100,000 and had no record of airing any paid TV ads, leads incumbent Rep. Scott DesJarlais, R-Tenn., by 277 votes in the latest count, and DesJarlais conceded the race on Nov. 16. Fox News Digital previously reported that Broderick spent under $100,000 compared to DesJarlais’ more than $500,000. The Associated Press has yet to formally call the race with 99% of the vote counted so far.

Is China Misreading the Moment?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations.
  • Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.
  • President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. He served as Director and Deputy Senior Director for China and Taiwan Affairs at the National Security Council from 2021 to 2024.

Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America.

When U.S. President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing. The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have declared a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Beneath the surface, however, the détente is beginning to crack.

According to recent reports, the relationship between Washington and Beijing looks remarkably different from the way it did a little over a year ago, when the two sides agreed to a truce in Busan, South Korea. In April 2025, Washington initiated the trade war by raising tariffs on China past 140 percent, and Beijing responded by restricting rare-earth exports later that month and threatening another cutoff that October. After Trump promptly backed down, the two leaders reached the deal in Busan: Washington would cap tariffs and suspend a specific export control regulation known as the Affiliates Rule in exchange for Beijing’s suspension of fresh export controls on minerals and magnets and the resumption of their normal flow to the United States. On that basis, both sides pursued a broad deescalation.

In a recent development, since then, the Trump administration has been notably accommodating. Washington has kept new tariffs at 12.5 percent, well below the 20-percent ceiling Beijing previously agreed to. It has let advanced AI chips flow to China and to Chinese cutouts in Southeast Asia and has not added a Chinese firm to the Entity List in over the year, the longest pause since 2008. It has withheld arms sales from and downgraded defense talks with Taiwan, cut back naval transits of the Taiwan Strait, and raised doubts about U.S. support in the event of a crisis. And it has offered only muted support to such allies as Japan and the Philippines in the face of escalating Chinese coercion. All the while, Trump has praised Xi as a “great leader” and extended rare courtesies, including by welcoming Xi on the tarmac when he arrived in Washington for a state visit in September, the first such greeting of a foreign leader in 60 years.

According to recent reports, beijing has appreciated this accommodating approach—and seized the opportunity to act more assertively. It has viewed the competitive pause as temporary, a product of China’s growing strength and Trump’s admiration for Xi, and as a way to buy time to build advantage before the next eruption of tensions. With Washington occupied by its war in Iran and humbled by defeat in the last round of the trade war, Beijing has throttled the supply of minerals and magnets to the United States, taken steps to ensure that its industrial and technological gains remain in China, and increased pressure on its neighbors.

It has been revealed that so far, Beijing has used the time well, advancing its objectives with little serious pushback from Washington. But China risks overreaching in its relationship with the United States. Not only is an incoming Democratic Congress likely to constrain Trump’s conciliatory China policy. There are also growing frustrations over Beijing’s unwillingness to fulfill the terms agreed to in Busan. Pressure on AI chips and export controls are emerging in the wake of revelations about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and his firm’s influence over U.S. export control policy. And upcoming U.S. policies in response to the scandal could provoke a response from Beijing.

Xi and Trump will meet in Shenzhen and again in December in Miami, but with the January expiration of the Busan agreement looming in the background (and with no summits planned for next year), time is running out for the two leaders to extend and strengthen the current truce. If the détente falls apart the next time Washington’s and Beijing’s interests clash, China will be better prepared. It may also, perhaps hubristically, be more willing to escalate.

Although China favors Washington’s current accommodating approach and hopes it will last as long as possible, Beijing is also confident that it is strengthening its hand for a more contentious future. For China’s leaders, the current détente has been less an end goal than a temporary intermission, a means to build leverage ahead of the next round of strategic competition and, ultimately, a decisive long-term advantage.

It has been revealed that prominent Chinese scholars see the calm that followed Busan as tactical rather than strategic. Chen Dongxiao, the president of the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, told the Shanghai news outlet The Paper that the two countries remain in a “tactical truce.” In May, Wu Xinbo of Fudan University told Beijing News, “If we can achieve a relationship of constructive strategic stability over the next three years, it will extend China’s period of strategic stability and win us time and space for development.” Writing in the journal International Review in August, he declared that the current “tactical stability” was “neither sustainable nor solid.” Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese foreign ministry official, was more blunt: “The more time we have, the better prepared we might be towards a final showdown on Taiwan or maybe another trade war.”.

Recent findings suggest that beijing attributes little of the stabilization to Washington. In his August essay, Wu wrote that it “is not the result of the U.S. side having a change of heart or showing goodwill, but was won by China through arduous striving and struggle.” The United States had no choice; it simply needed the “breathing room.” Wang Yong, the director of Peking University’s American Studies Center, described the trade war as “a tipping point in terms of strength.” The former editor of the Global Times, Hu Xijin, wrote in a Weibo post after the U.S. midterm elections that “the current equilibrium in U.S.-China relations is the result of a contest of strength.” As Wu told The Paper in September, Washington has come to understand that Beijing “needs to be treated equally and with respect” and that China is “bolder about ‘drawing its sword.’” Keeping the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets tight, to Beijing’s mind, might reinforce the current competitive pause rather than undermine it by reminding American leaders of China’s leverage.

Sources indicate that another critical factor in the current de-escalation, Chinese analysts argue, is Trump’s personality. Trump’s “distinct and unique decision-making style,” as Chen put it, has single-handedly blunted the more forceful defense of U.S. interests that members of his own administration and legislators in both parties favor. “He is often not entirely swayed by bipartisan opposition and still continues to pursue policies based on his own judgment,” Chen explained in the same interview. Writing in the Singaporean paper Lianhe Zaobao in September, Zhao Minghao of Fudan University more pointedly explained that Trump “admires power and prefers to engage with the leaders of powerful countries,” a stabilizing trait that benefits Beijing’s diplomacy while leaving allies and partners on the sidelines. “Of all modern U.S. presidents, Trump has cared the least about Taiwan,” one Guizhou-based commentator wrote. “He would readily sacrifice the island for his own interests.” An article reposted on the website of Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship journal, dwelt on Trump’s decision to greet Xi at the airport when he arrived for his state visit in September. The gesture, it claimed, “reflects the new historical position of China-U.S. relations.”.

But China also worries that Trump’s influence will decline over the next two years and perhaps cease altogether after 2028. Wang Hao, a professor at Fudan University’s Center for American Studies, told Phoenix News that the Democratic Party’s approach will not be “as pragmatic and flexible as the Trump administration’s,” a sentiment echoed across Chinese social media after the Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections.

The awareness that Trump’s approach may not survive beyond his presidency is precisely why Beijing has sought to lock it in through diplomacy. According to the Chinese readout, at the summit in May 2026, Xi declared that the relationship of “constructive strategic stability” he and Trump had agreed to build would provide guidance for U.S.-Chinese relations “over the next three years and beyond.” That duration was not accidental. As the scholar Zheng Yongnian put it at the time, the three-year window was “tailor-made for President Trump,” matching his current term. Beijing hopes it will bind his successor.

If diplomacy fails to secure U.S. deescalation, China hopes leverage will succeed. Over the last year, Beijing has used the time and space created by the détente to strengthen its position in industrial and technological competition with the United States. Beijing has long sought to make the world more dependent on China while reducing its own dependence on the world. But over the last year, that approach has evolved. Beijing has unveiled a raft of measures intended to ensure that its industrial, technological, and scientific know-how do not diffuse beyond China’s borders in order to lock in the country’s advantages.

To keep foreign firms in China and blunt Western countries’ leverage over the Chinese economy, the State Council issued Orders 834 and 835, which effectively threaten companies that cut ties with Chinese partners or seek to exit the country with the risk of investigation, exclusion from the Chinese market, exit bans on executives, and possible criminal prosecution. To keep talent in China, Beijing has authorized exit bans on citizens considered possible risks to industrial or technological security and, according to Bloomberg, now requires travel approval for top AI and chip specialists and their families. And to keep scientific discoveries in China, the Ministry of State Security has warned researchers that they must clear security reviews before submitting articles to foreign journals. China has also imposed or proposed new export controls on dozens of technologies, from mining and batteries to AI models and biotechnology in order to protect its industrial capabilities. Beijing has even worked to prevent the transfer of equipment and engineers to India and Southeast Asia, stalled battery ventures with Indian firms, undermined Apple’s effort to move manufacturing to India, and issued a sweeping regulation that subjects Chinese investment abroad to a national security review more expansive than the United States’ own outbound investment review.

In a recent development, beijing’s rare-earth licensing regime exemplifies China’s leverage-building strategy. To obtain a license, foreign buyers must hand over customer lists, the identities of their end owners, and images of their production lines, all of which gives China insight into Western dependencies and helps it uncover chokepoints it can squeeze. Beijing has threatened to use these powers against countries that seek to protect themselves from the flood of Chinese manufactured goods entering their markets. In July, Beijing highlighted how precise it can now be in applying pressure when it cut off 14 European firms, including the German arms maker Rheinmetall, from Chinese dual-use exports in retaliation for EU sanctions related to Chinese support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Beijing has paired these measures at home with escalating pressure campaigns in its near abroad, betting that a distracted and chastened Washington will not come to the aid of China’s neighbors. That campaign has been most brazen in the South China Sea, where China has engaged in escalations unseen before the détente. Since Busan, Beijing has essentially abrogated its 2024 understanding with the Philippines, which maintained stability on the question of Second Thomas Shoal. In July, a Chinese coast guard boat rammed a Philippine navy inflatable and its crew clubbed a sailor on the head with a wooden baton, the most violent assault on Philippine personnel in years.

Sources indicate that the timing of these incidents has been provocative. In July, when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio were in Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations meetings, the coast guard launched water-cannon attacks on Philippine vessels near Scarborough Shoal. Then, in September, during Xi’s U.S. state visit, Chinese warships and cutters blocked a Philippine resupply mission outright for the first time in two years. In October, Chinese cutters interfered with a medical evacuation from Second Thomas Shoal, delaying a patient transfer by ten hours. Last month, Beijing’s ambassador in Manila mused that if China chose to use force against the Philippines, “we may easily win.”.

China has also run its broadest coercion campaign against Japan in more than a decade, nominally in response to comments made by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Taiwan. It has included a travel advisory, a seafood ban, a dual-use export ban, and curbs on rare-earth exports that have forced Japanese companies to contemplate shutting down operations. Chinese carrier-based fighters have locked their weapons-targeting radar onto Japanese jets. Beijing has also pursued upcoming gas structures in the East China Sea and set a record 357-day coast guard presence in 2025 around the Japanese-administered Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands), with cutters now chasing Japanese fishing boats into territorial waters. Washington’s support for Tokyo has, so far, been limited.

And around Taiwan, China has made its pressure quieter but more routine. In December 2025, during the People’s Liberation Army’s Justice Mission exercises, China fired live rockets closer to Taiwan than ever before, landing ten of them inside the island’s 24-nautical-mile contiguous zone. As of this summer, Beijing has reduced air incursions, but coast guard activity around Taiwan’s outlying islands has become routinized. And since June, Beijing has run standing “law enforcement patrols” east of Taiwan, asserting jurisdiction over the waters Taipei would need in a blockade.

Outside of Asia, Beijing has sought to take advantage of anger, particularly in the developing world, at the Trump administration’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and the Iran war. Before traveling to Washington, Xi made a point of stopping in several capitals: he toured Bishkek and Cairo, and attended the BRICS summit in Latest Delhi, stressing that China, not the United States, is now the steadier partner.

In a recent development, beijing has reason to think this approach is working. It rightly judged that Washington would prioritize keeping the détente alive over responding to its provocations. A year after Busan, China holds a tighter grip on critical supply chains, has set upcoming precedents in Asia, and faces an adversary in Washington that has grown used to holding back. Beijing likely believes it is better off now than it was when the truce began.

What looks like success now, however, may still prove to be overreach. In addition to rare earths and magnets, several key questions went unresolved in past U.S.-Chinese summits and are likely to resurface in this week’s summit in Shenzhen, including China’s anticipated purchases of Boeing aircraft and agricultural products, AI safety, and the United States’ suspension of arms sales to Taiwan. But the most important question is what will become of the current trade truce.

According to recent reports, the United States has complied with the terms of the Busan agreement, suspending the Affiliates Rule and lowering tariffs, but Beijing has throttled the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets to the United States. U.S. officials say China has delivered only about two-thirds of what it promised, and trade data suggest the shortfall is larger still. The administration believes Beijing’s noncompliance is deliberate. Anecdotal evidence from American business leaders in regular touch with the Ministry of Commerce confirms the administration’s assessment that Beijing seeks to keep a tight leash on rare-earth minerals and will occasionally “yank the chain” on individual companies in response to any perceived slight by Washington.

According to recent reports, from the U.S. perspective, the very point of the Busan negotiations was to avoid this situation. Indeed, the U.S. fact sheet at Busan indicated that China agreed to issue general licenses for a number of rare earths and other critical minerals to American end users and their suppliers worldwide; case-by-case licenses, which could be delayed by Beijing, would not be required. China has not denied making that commitment, and a few weeks after the summit, the Ministry of Commerce began issuing a new category of general licenses to magnet makers. But Beijing’s licenses have been narrow and firm specific, and American industry continues to face enormous challenges in securing certain rare earths, notably yttrium and scandium.

Industry observers note that beijing’s intention may not be to undermine the Busan agreement but, paradoxically, to strengthen it. In keeping with its belief that strength begets American conciliation, China’s strategy appears to be to occasionally impose shortages to remind Washington of the leverage that Beijing continues to enjoy. But the tactic is beginning to backfire. Shortages of yttrium, used for jet engines and gas turbines, have forced some suppliers to suspend production. Chipmakers are running short of scandium. All of this strengthens the arguments of those who believe Beijing never intended to honor Busan and that the United States should begin to walk away from the agreement. If Washington concludes that China will weaponize rare earths no matter what the United States does, the case for American restraint may fall apart, and with it the détente that has bought Beijing the time it prizes.

Industry observers note that tensions are also mounting in other areas. Each side is increasingly frustrated with the other’s unilateral economic measures and restrictions on technology, particularly those that were not addressed in Busan: for Beijing, U.S. import controls, outbound investment regimes, and licensing backlogs; for Washington, Chinese export controls and State Council directives. A Democratic Congress is less likely to countenance Trump’s China policy and more likely to pursue investigations into China’s espionage and influence efforts and potential malfeasance at the Department of Commerce. The explosive controversy around Huang and Nvidia has the potential to inject fresh tensions into the relationship, particularly on matters related to AI and export controls. The Department of Commerce has already issued a new interim final rule to stop Chinese firms from smuggling chips into China or remotely accessing American AI chips in Southeast Asian data centers. Administration officials insist that closing a loophole China itself claims not to use “should not be something that generates countermeasures.” But Beijing may well retaliate before the rule takes effect in February.

Recent findings suggest that these headwinds make breakthroughs in Shenzhen on purchases, artificial intelligence, nuclear weapons, or Iran less likely. With the truce, extended last week by just two months, set to formally expire on January 10, the summit is one of the last opportunities for Trump and Xi to reach even a modest declaration that they are working to extend the terms set out in Busan and will aim to conclude negotiations in December, when Xi comes to Miami for the G-20 summit.

Sources indicate that if China were to continue to throttle rare-earth minerals and magnets, and a January breakdown did come to pass, the two sides might find themselves in another round of escalation. Xi may arrive at the two upcoming summits holding a stronger hand than he did in Busan. But his actions are gradually producing a counterpart with less room—and perhaps less reason—to keep folding.

Do Democrats Disagree?
