📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

House lawmakers on both sides of the aisle spoke to Fox News Digital about what they are most thankful for as they get ready to celebrate Thanksgiving with their families.

In November 1966, 12 American soldiers stationed at an isolated outpost in a Vietnamese war zone were about as far from a traditional Thanksgiving at home as they could get.

Industry observers note that their only means of resupply was by air. But the U.S. military was determined to get them Thanksgiving dinner anyway.

A mess sergeant at Bien Hoa prepared turkey and all the trimmings, packed the meal into insulated containers and sent it by helicopter into War Zone D, where three officers and nine enlisted men of a 5th Special Forces detachment sat down to Thanksgiving dinner, according to Defense Department records preserved by the National Archives.

The delivery was one piece of a massive logistical effort the U.S. military has undertaken during wars spanning generations to get traditional Thanksgiving meals to troops serving in combat zones.

Soldiers are pictured eating Thanksgiving dinner during World War I, in 1918. (National Archives).

From civilians sending tens of thousands of turkeys to Union troops during the Civil War to helicopters carrying hot meals to soldiers in Korea, the holiday has been observed through some of the nation's most consequential conflicts.

Thanksgiving became a national tradition in the midst of war. President Abraham Lincoln issued his 1863 Thanksgiving proclamation as the Civil War entered its third year, calling on Americans to observe the final Thursday of November as a day of "Thanksgiving and Praise.".

By the following year, Americans on the home front were mounting a massive effort to get Thanksgiving dinner to Union troops.

Former War Department official Charles A. Dana later recalled the "great turkey movement" of November 1864. In Latest York alone, organizers reported having 20,000 turkeys ready to send to the front, according to Dana's account. A Philadelphia committee sought transportation for another 4,000 destined for troops serving under Gen. Philip Sheridan.

Sources indicate that U.S. service members stationed at an airbase in Norfolk, England, select turkeys for their Thanksgiving dinners at a local farm on Nov. 6, 1943. (National Archives).

By World War II, the effort to put turkey on troops' Thanksgiving tables had grown so large that it affected whether Americans at home could find one for their own.

In August 1943, the War Food Administration restricted most civilian turkey sales as the government sought millions of pounds for the armed forces. An initial goal of at least 10 million pounds for troops overseas was expanded to include military installations at home, and the government ultimately obtained roughly 30 million pounds before the order was lifted in October, according to wartime government records.

A year later, delivering Thanksgiving dinner near the front could carry its own risks.

102-YEAR-OLD NAVY VETERAN STILL CRAVES HOT WINGS AFTER 102 COMBAT MISSIONS IN KOREA: 'I MIGHT MAKE IT TO 115'.

Sailors Leo F. DesJarlait, left, Eulice E. Wheeler, center, and G.J. Lindner eat turkey and trimmings at an advanced U.S. Navy base in the Aleutian Islands on Nov. 24, 1944. Lindner gives a "4.0" sign, meaning "perfect," in response to the Thanksgiving meal. (National Archives).

In Germany's Hürtgen Forest, Lt. Paul Boesch of the 121st Infantry Regiment later recalled being told that hot turkey dinners had arrived for his men amid some of the European campaign's most grueling fighting. Boesch protested that sending soldiers to collect the food would expose them to German artillery, but the order to distribute the meal stood.

His fears proved well-founded. As troops gathered to retrieve the food, German artillery struck the area, killing and wounding several men, according to Boesch's account.

Six years later, American troops were again eating Thanksgiving dinner near the front, this time in the bitter cold of North Korea.

In a recent development, on Thanksgiving Day 1950, Marines around the Chosin Reservoir were served turkey and cranberry sauce, candied sweet potatoes, fruitcake and mince pie. In the subzero temperatures, the food quickly began to freeze.

US NAVY RELEASES PHOTOS OF 'FRESH MEALS,' PUSHES BACK ON REPORTS OF FOOD SHORTAGES ON MIDDLE EAST WARSHIPS.

The dinner came as U.S. commanders remained optimistic that the war could soon be over. The following day, Gen. Douglas MacArthur released an offensive that became known as the "Home-by-Christmas" campaign.

It has been revealed that instead, Chinese forces entered the fighting in massive numbers. Within days of Thanksgiving, Marines around Chosin were surrounded and battling through one of the most brutal engagements of the Korean War.

Pfc. John A. Arnett, left, receives a turkey leg from Cpl. Fred Burks during Thanksgiving dinner in Korea on Nov. 22, 1951. The chow line was set up on the back side of a hill roughly 200 yards from the main line of resistance. (National Archives).

More than half a century later, another generation of American troops was spending Thanksgiving at war in Iraq and Afghanistan.

In 2003, President George W. Bush secretly flew into Baghdad to surprise roughly 600 troops gathered for Thanksgiving dinner at Baghdad International Airport. Air Force One approached with its cabin shades drawn and lights dimmed amid tight security surrounding the trip.

"I was just looking for a warm meal somewhere," Bush joked before addressing the troops and helping serve Thanksgiving dinner.

In Afghanistan, getting that dinner to troops stationed far from major bases could require a different kind of operation.

In a recent development, president George H.W. Bush eats Thanksgiving dinner on the hood of a Humvee while visiting U.S. troops in Saudi Arabia during Operation Desert Shield on Nov. 22, 1990. (National Archives).

On Thanksgiving 2007, helicopters carried turkeys and traditional fixings from Bagram Airfield to soldiers at remote firebases in the Tagab Valley, according to a contemporaneous U.S. military account.

It was the first hot meal some of the soldiers had eaten in months. Because the positions still had to be defended, troops rotated between Thanksgiving dinner and standing watch.

Industry observers note that "The white meat was magnificent," Pfc. Matt Lorimer of the 82nd Airborne Division remarked.

President George W. Bush traveled to Iraq in 2003 to meet with troops without the public's knowledge. (Tim Sloan/AFP/Getty Images).

Recent findings suggest that at another remote Afghan outpost two years later, troops spent a month fattening five scrawny turkeys purchased locally for Thanksgiving. But five birds were not enough to feed roughly 150 soldiers.

Sources indicate that additional turkey was flown from the United States to Bagram Airfield and then transported to the outpost. Even that was not the end of the journey.

The Real Nvidia Scandal

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that vivek Chilukuri is Senior Fellow and Director of the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Upcoming American Security.
  • Industry observers note that how China Exploited a Massive Loophole in U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that emily Kilcrease is Senior Fellow and Director of the Energy, Economics, and Security Program at the Center for a New American Security. From 2019 to 2021, first in the Trump administration and then in the Biden administration, she was Deputy Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Investment.

Industry observers note that vivek Chilukuri is Senior Fellow and Director of the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Upcoming American Security. He previously served as Legislative Director to Senator Michael Bennet and as a policy adviser at the U.S. Department of State.

Industry observers note that how China Exploited a Massive Loophole in U.S. National Security—and How Congress Can Close It.

Emily Kilcrease and Vivek Chilukuri.

Sources indicate that the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia this week added another twist to a scandal that has transfixed Washington and Silicon Valley. The stakes go beyond the swings of the stock market or the salacious details about Huang’s affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed and a potential Chinese asset. At its core, the scandal has exposed something that matters far more than any one man or firm: American export-control policy remains riddled with loopholes, hobbled by incapacity and infighting, and divorced from clear strategy. Unless Washington fixes this, it risks imperiling the United States’ hard-won advantage in artificial intelligence.

This export policy failure is more than the sum of specific deficiencies. It stems from the Trump administration’s broader posture on China. Washington has embraced unfettered AI acceleration at the same time as it has struck a more accommodating stance toward Beijing. That combination set the stage for the explosive Megaspeed scandal—and perhaps others that have yet to emerge. As a result, China has been able to access an alarming number of advanced chips that have enabled it to narrow the AI gap with the United States and power its AI-driven military modernization. According to the AI research institute Epoch AI, up to a third of China’s AI computing power may come from smuggled chips. China’s top AI models are now just months behind the U.S. frontier. The narrow gap reflects China’s genuine innovation and access to abundant energy resources as well as its relentless efforts to circumvent U.S. controls.

Industry observers note that huang’s return to Nvidia at the behest of President Donald Trump suggests that both the tech giant and the White House seem utterly uninterested in keeping powerful AI chips from China. It will instead fall to Congress to ensure that the United States leverages its compute advantage and maintains its AI edge. The midterm elections and mounting bipartisan concerns over the Megaspeed debacle give Congress new momentum to correct course. Its near-term agenda should include closing known loopholes that played a key role in allowing Megaspeed to supply advanced chips to China, stepping up enforcement of existing controls, and strengthening oversight of the administration’s export-control decisions.

Over the medium term, Congress must also tackle the broader question of how to balance the strategic benefits of exporting U.S. technology to build the world’s AI infrastructure with robust controls to prevent its leakage to China. The long-standing debate over which American AI chips and capabilities Washington should permit to diffuse globally and under what conditions has finally boiled over into the mainstream—and, in a perverse way, the national security community can thank Alice Huang for forcing the glitch.

The issue before Congress, however, is much broader than addressing the specifics of the Nvidia scandal. Congress must also contend with the underlying impulses driving the administration’s China policy and install guardrails to avoid the erosion of U.S. export controls. This means that after Congress passes near-term bills to mop up the Megaspeed mess, it must then take the reins on setting long-term export-control strategy.

In a recent development, congress cannot stand by idly as AI blazes forward. OpenAI’s top model can now perform professional tasks as well as or better than humans 85 percent of the time, up from just 14 percent in 2024. The time an AI model can independently work on a task is doubling every four months. Last week, a researcher at Anthropic revealed that AI helped him untangle the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous problems in pure mathematics.

According to recent reports, as capabilities have grown, so have risks. Frontier models can now complete simulated cyberattacks on networks on their own, and hackers are using AI models to partially automate their attacks. In the July incident involving the AI platform Hugging Face, rogue AI agents escaped their testing environment and plotted to evade human oversight, underscoring the difficulty of aligning model behavior with human intent. The growing power of AI and the risks from misuse or loss of control make U.S. leadership a national security imperative.

At its core, the U.S.-Chinese AI competition boils down to which country can deploy the best chips in the highest quantities to train and adopt advanced AI models. The Biden administration’s controls slowed Chinese AI developers by leaving them with fewer, worse chips. Nvidia’s top Blackwell chips are nearly seven times better than Huawei’s Ascend equivalents. By the end of 2026, Huawei will likely have produced less than four percent of the compute that Nvidia will have over the same time. As the founder and CEO of DeepSeek, one of China’s top AI companies, admitted in 2024, “Our problem has never been money—it’s the embargo on high-end chips.”.

In a recent development, to circumvent Biden-era restrictions, elaborate networks for smuggling and transshipment emerged to divert chips to China from other countries that could legally acquire them, and Chinese companies leveraged export-control loopholes to remotely access U.S.-powered compute through data centers abroad. Chinese firms funded companies such as Megaspeed to facilitate these workarounds. Backed by the Chinese tech giant Alibaba, Megaspeed has purchased $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips since 2023, prompting an investigation from the U.S. government. Chinese companies also used a technique known as adversarial distillation—training their models on the outputs of top U.S. models at a fraction of the compute. All of this needlessly shrank the United States’ AI lead over China, even after the imposition of export controls.

Sources indicate that these developments should have spurred the Trump administration to better resource, enforce, and patch the export controls when it came into office. It did the opposite. In May 2025, the administration suspended the Biden administration’s AI Diffusion Rule, which had established rules for which countries could access advanced chips and in what quantities. Then, after initially prohibiting sales to China of Nvidia’s H20 chip, which was custom-built as a less powerful product for the Chinese market, the Trump administration reversed course in December 2025 and greenlighted the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chip. Although the H200 is two generations behind top U.S. chips, it remains superior to anything China can produce. An investigation from the House Foreign Affairs Committee in November revealed that between December 2025 and May 2026, the Trump administration approved the sale of more than 800,000 of Nvidia’s H200 chips and AMD’s MI325X equivalent, including to companies that the Pentagon has designated as linked to the Chinese military. This week, under pressure from Congress, the administration added Megaspeed to the entity list, which blocks those listed from buying U.S. products without a license—but before that, the administration had not added a single latest individual or business to the list in 2026.

According to recent reports, this regulatory vacuum and policy incoherence created the perfect conditions for Megaspeed. The Singaporean firm at the center of the Nvidia scandal seems tailor-made to operate in the seams of U.S. export controls. In 2024, the Commerce Department initiated a formal investigation of the manufacturer, which could have led to sanctions such as being placed on the entity list. But the Trump administration dragged its feet in pursuing the investigation. In the meantime, Megaspeed stocked Southeast Asian data centers with thousands of U.S. chips, enabling remote access for Chinese firms. This remote access loophole in U.S. export controls was a well-known and increasingly popular workaround for China-linked firms, but the Trump administration left it open for nearly two years and closed it only last week amid pressure from the Nvidia scandal. Regardless of the Megaspeed specifics, the net result of the Trump administration’s actions and inaction is that China has enjoyed access to far more computing power than it should have during a vital period of the AI competition.

The administration’s long-awaited closure of the remote access loophole is a welcome step. The rule requires foreign data centers to secure a license before offering significant computing power to China-based customers. It also requires a license to export advanced chips to places that could facilitate remote access and chip diversion, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. This rule will make it harder for firms such as Megaspeed to import chips in the first place, or to use them to serve China-based customers. But the rule will be difficult to enforce because the U.S. Commerce Department does not have the legal authority under export controls to directly regulate services such as cloud computing. More important, the administration’s lax enforcement of past controls—and internal divisions over the new ones—raise serious questions about its willingness to follow through. Huang’s reinstatement as CEO, with Trump’s backing, will make it harder to vigorously enforce these new controls and move toward a tougher posture on China.

Since Congress cannot rely on the administration to fix export controls and protect the United States’ AI lead, lawmakers should urgently advance bipartisan measures to address the underlying conditions that gave rise to entities such as Megaspeed. As a starting point, Congress should pass the Remote Access Security Act, which would give the administration clear legal authority for controlling remote access to data centers powered by U.S. compute. While implementation will require close congressional oversight, getting the right legal structure in place is an important first step. Next, it should work with industry and technical experts to fund and fast-track “on-chip” technologies—basically, features that can verify a chip’s location and counter smuggling and diversion. Beyond sorting out the technical feasibilities, Congress will need to work with industry to understand the implications of on-chip security mechanisms for global competitiveness and the potential surveillance risks should China develop similar controls since it produces much of the world’s legacy chips.

Along with these technical fixes, Congress should seize on the Megaspeed scandal to strengthen oversight. The AI Overwatch Act, which may be included in the annual defense bill, would codify existing export controls on advanced chips into law, preventing the current or a future administration from reversing them. It would also empower Congress to review and block advanced chips sales to U.S. adversaries. Congress can go even further by establishing a upcoming investigative committee or inspector general to strengthen oversight of sensitive chip export-control policies. Together, these actions would go a long way toward combating the circumvention that let firms such as Megaspeed thrive.

Sources indicate that at the same time, closing loopholes and codifying rules is insufficient to fix the underlying issues that led to the Megaspeed scandal in the first place. This mess is directly downstream from Trump’s dovish shift on China that has seen the administration take a softer line on Beijing just as the AI race accelerated. The administration’s own overreach forced Washington into a conciliatory posture. Administration officials failed to realize that China had learned its lesson from the first Trump administration’s trade wars and was poised to retaliate hard in the second term. After China responded to Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and export controls with its own punishing controls on rare earths, the Trump administration found its way into a vaguely defined and fragile truce. This has severely constrained U.S. policymaking, including related to compute controls.

It has been revealed that indeed, Trump became an easy sell for advocates of aggressive AI promotion such as Jensen Huang. This camp argues that U.S. leadership in the global AI race requires pushing American AI technologies to as many parts of the globe as possible—including China. They claim that keeping China “addicted” to the U.S. AI stack gives Washington leverage and outweighs the national security concerns that could come with helping China improve its AI capabilities. Huang even pushed demonstrably false narratives that China’s military was not interested in Nvidia’s chips and labeled his critics as “unpatriotic” for not wanting U.S. chips spread as far and wide as possible and therefore depriving American tech firms of global market share.

Trump, who was interested in stabilizing the relationship with China and prioritizing near-term, transactional victories on trade, bought it. He also broke with decades of U.S. foreign policy precedent to negotiate export controls with China. In a series of “do nothing” leader-level meetings since, the president has emphasized summitry optics over pushing China on any sensitive challenges. And Huang’s restoration at Nvidia ensures that the president’s worst impulses on China will continue to be egged on by his favored tech CEO, to the detriment of U.S. national security.

It has been revealed that A core part of Congress’s longer-term agenda should be outlining the basic principles to determine who can import or remotely access advanced AI chips and under what conditions. Administrations have gone back and forth over this line-drawing exercise. The Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule would have imposed a global licensing regime that controlled not just the export of chips but also the aggregate U.S.-powered compute that any country could receive. Under Trump, only a handful of countries face restrictions. A smarter approach would condition advanced chip sales on the buyer’s ability to protect them from diversion and guard against misuse by malign actors looking to skirt safety and security rules. Allied and partner governments could demonstrate this by developing robust economic security policies to prevent chip diversion or remote access. Foreign companies would have to show strong compliance and security commitments. In practice, this would mean having internal procedures to ensure that chips are not diverted and maintaining cooperation with Commerce Department officials to verify that such procedures were working.

It has been revealed that congress can also help rebuild allies’ confidence in U.S. export-control policy. There was hard-won, if imperfect, progress on allied alignment in key areas of export controls under the Biden administration, notably with the Dutch and the Japanese on controls of semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The painstaking work needed to get allies on board can be agonizingly slow, but once achieved, it is far more likely to endure than if the United States imposes extraterritorial controls over their objections. The MATCH Act, one of the bills revived following the Megaspeed scandal, requires controls on allied-produced tools if Washington is unable to negotiate allied alignment. It is a rather rude approach at a moment when U.S. export controls seem to be on shaky footing, U.S. tariffs against allies have pushed relations to a near breaking point, and allies rightly question whether the United States still views China as a strategic threat. Instead, Congress should support efforts to create durable frameworks for allied alignment, such as economic security agreements in key strategic sectors.

It has been revealed that A longer-term agenda must include fixing the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, the main agency responsible for administering and enforcing export controls. The bureau has been gutted by dismissals and low morale during the Trump administration, but it has been underresourced for far longer. Congress should increase funding and require modernization of the bureau’s antiquated IT system. Just as key, Congress needs to help insulate policymaking decisions from corporate influence, and it can help by insisting that future Commerce Department officials commit to independent and risk-based decision-making to earn confirmation.

None of these steps will be easy. The president’s support of Huang’s restoration indicates that stock market fluctuations weigh more heavily in his decision-making than national security, and the administration is unlikely to welcome increased congressional oversight. The Constitution gives the executive wide deference on matters of foreign policy and national security. But Congress has a role in ensuring that the president faithfully executes the laws and is supported by the right resources, oversight, and strategic priorities. The United States’ AI lead may hinge on whether it meets the moment.

Robin Wigglesworth (Portfolio, 416 pp., $35, September 2026).

According to recent reports, I imagine there are likely only two reactions when readers stumble across a book such as A Fabulous Debt, a 1,000-year tale of bond market magic and mischief: Shoot me now, or straight into my veins. I’m in the latter camp, and unabashedly so. This is a fantastically entertaining read, and no holiday is complete, in our household at least, without in-depth discussions of financial crises dating back centuries.

According to recent reports, robin Wigglesworth’s book is so much fun to read because it is a fast-paced, exhaustively researched history of the driest subject in the world written in the most engaging way possible. Bonds—debt that pays interest, and that finances governments and companies—are actually the secret to understanding the whims and vagaries of everything that has happened since Venice was on the upswing in the pre-Renaissance years to the latest market meltdown over U.S. President Donald Trump’s wild policies. There is literally nothing more central, and perhaps less well understood, to the world today, and Wigglesworth is the worthiest of sherpas.

According to recent reports, beyond all the financial innovation—which was much, and often not even criminal—the characters alone are amazing. From 12th-century Venetian doges to Alexander Hamilton to 19th-century rail barons to 1980s bond villains, and then, just a few decades later, even more creative bond villains. This is the prequel to The Big Short.

If I were a ratings agency, I would give the book an AAA+.

Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff (Harper, 256 pp., $30, April 2026).

In a recent development, A guide for the perplexed? I feel seen; count me in.

Sources indicate that just as there was once Fordism—the shorthand homage to Henry Ford and 20th-century capitalism that married mass production with mass consumption—our current era of bewilderment probably needed its own -ism. Enter Elon Musk. Co-authors Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff make the case that Muskism is a worldview that offers an “operating system” for our times. But you, dear reader, are not just partaking in Musk’s OS by buying his cars or renting his internet. You are becoming part of his universe. “Trying to unplug from Musk,” the book points out, “you realize he owns the socket.”.

According to recent reports, this is a slim, urgent, and highly readable book on the man who thinks he is the world’s most notable being. It is also about what Musk’s rise means for the rest of us—the permanently perplexed—whose tax dollars fueled his ambitions, who watched as he gutted the federal government, and who continue to wonder why we’re developing flying cars when all our actual flights are delayed. Mercifully, unlike some other works on Musk, this is no hagiography. Instead, it charts out how Musk came about his views and how his techno-maximalist, anti-humanitarian venom came to poison much of Silicon Valley.

Sources indicate that catherine E. De Vries and Alexandros Kentikelenis (Oxford University Press, 256 pp., $34.99, October 2026).

Who in their right mind would read a book about the European Union during a holiday? Well, think twice. How Europe Survives by Catherine E. De Vries and Alexandros Kentikelenis is one of the more upbeat books you will ever read about the subject. From their perches in Madrid and Milan, the two political scientists explain why the crises that have plagued Europe in the past two decades—such as the eurozone crisis, refugee crisis, Brexit, the war in Ukraine, and the COVID-19 pandemic—have not killed the EU, as many predicted.

In a recent development, in their telling, Europe is like a living mechanism. It improvises and adapts to its circumstances, albeit slowly. With each crisis, Europe’s leaders face a choice: Fall in the precipice or seek compromise. So far, they have opted for the latter. The result is often far from pretty, but as the book reminds us, these compromises generally produce a quality of life, stability, and moderation that make some other nations green with envy.

—Caroline de Gruyter, FP columnist.

Emily St. John Mandel (Knopf, 320 pp., $32, September 2026).

Recent findings suggest that it felt like the world was ending most weeks this year. “BREAKING: EVERYTHING” was a pithy summation of that time the planes were grounded and Microsoft Outlook sputtered to a halt. (I’m sure as you read this, fresh hells will have presented themselves.) Amid such systemic collapse, the concept of a dystopic sci-fi novel set in the smoldering ruins of an American civil war was not appealing—until I read a review of Exit Party that mentioned it was “cozy.”.

The novel, which begins with a really bad party off the Sunset Strip in the newly formed Republic of California, courses with adrenaline but never resignation. With a dash of the Bourne movies and a soupcon of fellow Canuck Margaret Atwood, Emily St. John Mandel invokes our worst nightmares and then uses them as a mere backdrop to an absorbing story about art, friendship, and love, asking, “Who will you be at the end of the world?”.

Wil Haygood (Knopf, 384 pp., $35, February 2026).

By bringing readers deeply into the experiences of African American soldiers during the Vietnam War, Wil Haygood’s The War Within a War confronts us with the reality of the socioeconomic and racial inequality so often at the heart of modern warfare, and especially of its American variants.

Through individual stories that come to life on the page, Haygood documents how Black soldiers were disproportionately represented on the battlefield in Vietnam, and how these soldiers were disproportionately killed and wounded early in the war. Yet they were promoted to positions of command in numbers well beneath those that their presence on the front lines would have suggested. He also highlights the indifferent treatment that Black veterans commonly experienced upon their discharge, when many faced few options beyond returning to poverty-ravaged inner-city neighborhoods, where jobs were scarce and cheap narcotics plentiful.

Haygood’s book joins a growing literature about the bitter irony of African American soldiers fighting, from the U.S. Revolution and the Civil War to the present, for the freedom and full citizenship of others, even as they have been denied these things or discriminated against themselves.

—Howard W. French, FP columnist.

Robin Yassin-Kassab (Saqi Books, 352 pp., $27.95, September 2026).

Sources indicate that not long after the Syrian uprising began in 2011, I started receiving email installments of Robin Yassin-Kassab’s blog, Qunfuz. I had never heard of him, but his searing and eloquent takes on Syria ensured that I did not send Qunfuz to my junk folder. So, when I saw that Yassin-Kassab had written a book, it was an easy preorder.

In a recent development, the Blood Between Us is not an eyewitness account. Yassin-Kassab is of Syrian and Scottish descent, lives in the United Kingdom, and only made a few relatively brief forays into Syria during its 14-year conflict. This is actually to the volume’s benefit, however. Yassin-Kassab offers both the intimacy of the bloodletting as told to him by his interlocutors and an analytic detachment that provides perspective on the Syrian revolution as it unfolded.

Sources indicate that his central point is that the Syrian people’s triumph in December 2024 was not the bolt from the blue that it seemed. Despite the static battlefield, repression, displacement, and death, the uprising against the Assad regime never ended. Admittedly, The Blood Between Us is not an uplifting holiday read, so maybe hold off for a few weeks—but do not miss it.

Robert Jackson Bennett (Del Rey, 400 pp., $32, August 2026).

It has been revealed that the most entertaining book I’ve read this year was Robert Jackson Bennett’s A Trade of Blood, the third in his ongoing series of fantasy detective stories. Bennett’s tales of a cantankerous master detective and her long-suffering, curious sidekick are an exercise in how to keep sequels fresh—and also examinations of the dilemmas of power and the double-sidedness of a government trying to do good things through troublesome means. They can stand with some of the best of Golden Age detective literature, but they also have giant monsters.

Eli Clifton and Ian Lustick (Atria/One Signal Publishers, 304 pp., $29, August 2026).

My holiday recommendation is Eli Clifton and Ian Lustick’s Israel’s Lobby: America in the Grip of a Foreign Power. Israel’s rightward shift, ever-expanding occupation, and Gaza genocide have produced a sea-change in U.S. attitudes toward Israel. Yet Democratic and Republican politicians continue to give Israel nearly unconditional support and diplomatic protection, even when Israel defies U.S. wishes or takes actions that harm U.S. interests. Clifton and Lustick explain this puzzle by showing how hard-line pro-Israel individuals and groups have taken advantage of the lax campaign financing rules created by the 2010 Citizens United decision to keep politicians on board.

Having lost the battle for public opinion, the Israel lobby now relies primarily on raw political muscle, mostly in the form of money. (The recent midterm elections suggest this tactic may be beginning to backfire). Clifton and Lustick also describe how Israel’s most ardent defenders have used false charges of antisemitism to silence criticism of Israel, which poses broader threats to freedom of speech. If you’re curious why the United States keeps landing in quagmires in the Middle East, this book provides part of the answer.

Roger Berkowitz (Yale University Press, 176 pp., $28, October 2026).

At a time when political disagreement can be reason to end a friendship, Roger Berkowitz makes the case that democracy depends on our ability to nurture relationships across deep divides. In A World We Share, Berkowitz, the director of the Hannah Arendt Center at Bard College, offers an anatomy of Arendt’s friendships, which spanned fierce intellectual disagreements and profound moral differences.

Industry observers note that arendt’s circle included figures as disparate as the novelist Mary McCarthy, philosopher Karl Jaspers, and her one-time lover Martin Heidegger, whose embrace of Nazism tested the limits of a friendship with Arendt, a Jewish survivor of Adolf Hitler’s persecution. Berkowitz draws on Arendt’s extensive correspondence, including detailed epistolary exchanges on subjects as diverse as the Holocaust, Watergate, and marital infidelity. Through these relationships, Berkowitz makes the case that democracy depends upon worldviews grounded in mutual respect, spirited debate, and a willingness to break bread, exchange ideas, and forge emotional bonds with people whose convictions we reject.

His argument speaks to a moment when ideological certainties and litmus tests increasingly crowd out curiosity, and political differences can eclipse our ability to see common humanity, much less make common cause. As our politics enters a newly introduced and more hopeful phase, and as families and friends gather at holiday tables, this timely book is an invitation to rediscover the democratic necessity of friendship across divides.

Sources indicate that C. Thi Nguyen (Penguin Press, 368 pp., $32, January 2026).

Sources indicate that the Score, by philosopher C. Thi Nguyen, is a love letter to games, but it is also a surprising treatise on bureaucracy. The book interrogates how so much of modern life has become an exercise of keeping score through data, metrics, and rankings. That focus on the quantitative, Nguyen argues, can produce beauty and fun in a game, yet it can warp behavior to disastrous effect everywhere else.

In a recent development, in public policy, scorekeeping allows governments to create order and track progress in a sprawling, messy world, but often at the expense of context or nuance. Among Nguyen’s case studies is the work of anthropologist Sally Engle Merry on the U.S. State Department’s sex-trafficking report, which, by judging countries by their conviction rates, incentivized greater policing over reducing poverty.

For all its insights on processes and institutions, the book is also a joyous, sensual celebration of rock-climbing, fly-fishing, yo-yoing, and other pursuits that resist the gamification and optimization so characteristic of today’s world.

—Megan DuBois, associate editor.

Tareq Baconi (Washington Square Press, 256 pp., $19, October 2026, paperback).

Recent findings suggest that after I gifted Fire in Every Direction to a friend earlier this year, she sent me a message thanking me for the “novel”; she had read the first few pages and was immediately engrossed. Her misperception speaks to how engagingly Tareq Baconi narrates his own coming-of-age story—it reads like a bildungsroman, but it’s all true.

Industry observers note that baconi is a leading expert on Hamas, which he has previously written about for FP. In Fire in Every Direction, he takes a step back from his academic perch to reflect on his at-times painful journey to self-acceptance as a gay Palestinian man. Since his childhood in Amman, Jordan, Baconi had an intangible sense that he was different from his peers. His unrequited infatuation with a male classmate led to a broader reckoning within his family about sexuality and shame.

To escape Amman’s stifling conservatism, Baconi chose to attend university in London. Although there’s no love lost between him and Jordan—where his twice-displaced Palestinian parents begrudgingly fled to from Beirut during Lebanon’s civil war—he eventually finds his way back to Palestine. Rather than challenge his devotion to the Palestinian cause, Baconi’s queer identity affirms his commitment to securing liberation for all people.

David M. Sacks (Henry Holt and Co., 528 pp., $36.99, November 2026).

The Realist is a lucid, compelling, and granular biography of Hans Morgenthau, one of the most influential scholars of international politics in the immediate postwar era. David M. Sacks’ deft book provides a complete sweep of Morgenthau’s life and career from a small, provincial town in Germany to the global metropolis of Fresh York.

Sources indicate that A German-Jewish émigré who had direct experience of the rising tides of vicious antisemitism, Morgenthau succeeded after tireless efforts to find a professorship at the University of Chicago. After an illustrious career, he moved to the City College of New York, where he quickly became a fixture of the city’s intellectual establishment. As a public intellectual, Morgenthau was also an early and vociferous critic of the Vietnam War, despite harboring a deep-seated hostility toward the Soviet Union.

Sonia Gandhi (Knopf, $28, 544 pp., November 2026).

Sonia Gandhi is one of the most fascinating living political leaders in South Asia, but also one of its least understood. She rose from humble beginnings in Italy to become the scion of India’s biggest family dynasty, even becoming linked with India’s independence (her late husband Rajiv was the grandson of the country’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru). But this remarkable life trajectory also led to great tragedy, due to the assassinations of her mother-in law, Indira, in 1984, and of Rajiv in 1991.

Gandhi, who turns 80 next month, has always been very private about her personal life and rarely opens up publicly. We haven’t had a true sense of her life and how it has shaped her. Belonging, her latest memoir released earlier this month, tells a story that many in India and beyond have long wanted to hear.

—Michael Kugelman, FP’s South Asia Brief writer.

Saleem Haddad (Europa Editions, 336 pp., $19, February 2026).

Sources indicate that one of the most memorable novels I read this year was Saleem Haddad’s Floodlines, a multigenerational epic that stretches from Baghdad to London and elsewhere between. The three Iraqi British sisters at its center—who are variously estranged—are pulled back together by the discovery of lost artwork by their late father, a renowned painter.

The family that Haddad sketches feels real enough that a reader might be tricked into thinking the characters are loosely fictionalized. (The author drew on the story of his own great-uncle, an Iraqi modernist painter, for inspiration.) Even with elements of magical realism at play, Floodlines is ultimately rooted in the political and cultural history of Iraq.

The book reaches its climax in 2014, with the Islamic State on the rise. As an unlikely plot brings its characters back home, Haddad manages to strike a genuine note of hope against a backdrop of conflict, exile, and rupture. And despite the family dysfunction driving it, Floodlines would make an excellent gift for a close relative or friend.

—Audrey Wilson, managing editor.

Roger Zakheim (Regnery History, 472 pp., $40, November 2026).

Recent findings suggest that most accounts of U.S. President Ronald Reagan’s foreign policy focus on his high-level summitry and arms control agreements with Soviet Premier Mikhail Gorbachev. But in Peace Through Strength, Roger Zakheim, the director of the Reagan Institute, tells the story of his military buildup. Zakheim argues that Reagan was able to sustain the largest peacetime military expansion in U.S. history across two presidential terms in the face of stiff opposition, even from his own party, because he saw it as essential to his Cold War strategy.

As the free world faces threats from a new axis of aggressors, Trump calls for a record $1.5 trillion U.S. defense budget, and allied governments in NATO and the Indo-Pacific pledge to spend up to 5 percent of GDP on defense, democratic leaders are once again vexed by the question of how to maintain public and parliamentary support for a yearslong peacetime rearmament program. They would be well served to learn from Reagan’s successful example.

Catherine Liu (Verso, 192 pp., $24.95, September 2026).

According to recent reports, I was inspired to read Catherine Liu’s Traumatized after Gregory Jones-Katz’s excellent review of the book in FP—and it was every bit as compelling as promised. Not since Lauren Berlant’s 2011 classic Cruel Optimism have I encountered such a thoughtful treatment of society’s obsession with trauma narratives and the ways they impede our understanding of, and appetite for, political change.

Liu, a cultural theorist at the University of California, Irvine, examines the ways that social media has amplified these narratives, which have come to pervade the political spectrum, contributing to, among other things, inequality, apathy, and the death of liberalism.

It’s not light reading, per se, but it’s provocative, elegantly written, and deeply relevant to our current moment.

Ryan Gingeras (Avid Reader Press / Simon & Schuster, 416 pp., $35, February 2026).

Recent findings suggest that here is the story of the 20th century told from the other side of the law. In Mafia, historian Ryan Gingeras shows how organized crime made the United States and how the United States in turn remade organized crime on a global scale through its economic might, law enforcement efforts, and popular culture. From early Balkan brigands through the last season of Narcos, this wide-ranging and fast-moving account takes readers on a journey through the dark shadows of globalization.

Mohammed Soliman (Polity, 272 pp., $24.95, February 2026).

In the Washington lexicon, the term “Middle East” often conjures up images of protracted wars, militant groups, and failed U.S. attempts at nation-building. In his latest book, analyst Mohammed Soliman argues that moving past these quagmires requires reframing how the region is viewed entirely. Enter “West Asia,” a term that places the region at the edge of the world’s largest continent in lieu of its original Eurocentric conception.

Anchoring his thesis in the evolving ties among the wealthy Arab Gulf states, Israel, India, Egypt, and Japan—to name a few—Soliman argues that Washington should build a new regional order connecting the old Middle East to the Indo-Pacific predicated on realpolitik, technology, and shared security incentives.

In a recent development, A caveat: The book was published weeks before the United States launched its protracted war against Iran, which has injected more uncertainty into the prospect of Soliman’s proposed order. But rather than negating the book’s thesis, the Iran war has only underscored the importance of a new and provocative blueprint for what could come next.

U.S. Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer (D-NY), center, is seen here meeting with newly elected Democratic Senators, (L-R) Senator-elect Andy Kim (D-NJ), Senator-elect Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Senator-elect Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD) Senator-elect Adam Schiff (D-CA) Senator-elect Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE) and Senator-elect Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) at the U.S. Capitol Building on November 12, 2024. That group of senators is pushing to add an incoming freshman senator to the leadership ranks. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/Getty Images North America hide caption.

A group of Senate Democrats elected in 2024 sent a letter to colleagues Tuesday proposing to add an incoming freshman to the leadership ranks.

In a recent development, "The Freshman Representative to Leadership would be elected by members of the incoming freshman class and confirmed by the Conference," the letter mentioned. "We intend to request a vote on this proposal.".

It has been revealed that the letter, first reported by Politico, is signed by California Sen. Adam Schiff, Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, and Newly introduced Jersey Sen. Andy Kim.

The letter nods to the diverse class of incoming freshmen who helped catapult the party to controlling both chambers of Congress.

In a recent development, "These freshmen have their fingers on the pulse of long-time Democratic voters, those who voted for Democrats for the first time this past Election Day, and everyone in-between," the letter reads. "The deserve a seat at the table.".

Senate Democrats have been signaling a desire to uplift newly introduced voices in the party.

According to recent reports, "On election night, people voted very clearly for a newly introduced generation of leadership. That was very, very clear," Slotkin said during remarks at a conference of Democrats after the midterms.

In a recent development, new Jersey Sen. Cory Booker told MS NOW that leadership extends beyond the top post.

"This is a time for new leadership," Booker said, mentioning wanting to see more of incoming Sens. Annie Andrews of South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas. "I want to see them out front, I want to see them taking concerns, I want to see them running on the field.".

The proposed rule change comes ahead of the leadership election next week. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the majority leader.

Senate leadership is comprised not only of the top position of Majority leader but of additional conference officers. Both Van Hollen and Schumer support the idea of adding a position for a freshman to that leadership group.

"Leader Schumer was already planning to do this and is incredibly supportive of the idea," a spokesperson told NPR.

In a recent development, on Tuesday, Van Hollen posted to social media: "There should be a freshman senator on the Senate leadership team. As I've remarked, we need a new way to organize so we can deliver for the American people.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces intense public backlash, and Staten Island crowd members booed him at a recent event. National correspondent Bryan Llenas reports on independent estimates showing Mamdani's free universal child care program could cost $9.3 billion dollars, fifty-five percent more than claimed.

Newly introduced York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani approved roughly $850,000 in pay raises for dozens of City Hall aides during his first year in office, according to municipal payroll records reviewed by the New York Post.

The records show the raises were distributed to at least 46 staffers since Mamdani took office in January, bringing total compensation increases near $1 million.

The Post counted 21 fresh hires who received raises totaling $450,000 before their first anniversary on the job, more than twice the combined number of first-year employees who got raises under Eric Adams and Bill de Blasio.

Industry observers note that mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks to reporters in front of a painting of Alexander Hamilton about the city's finances during a news conference in New York Feb. 17, 2026. (Seth Wenig/AP Photo).

MAMDANI TURNS ON LATEST YORK CITY TEACHERS UNION WITH LAWSUIT BLOCKING PAY RAISES FOR EDUCATORS.

Sources indicate that on Jan. 28, five City Hall employees were granted salary increases totaling $95,000 on the same day Mamdani confirmed Upcoming York City faced an estimated $12 billion budget deficit, the records show. The mayor’s office later lowered that projected deficit to approximately $5.4 billion.

The mayor’s office on Nov. 12 confirmed the city’s fiscal 2027 budget rose $3.3 billion from the budget adopted in June, reaching $129.2 billion.

MAMDANI'S TAXPAYER-FUNDED INFLUENCER ARMY ACCUSED OF PLOTTING PRESSURE CAMPAIGN AGAINST NYC CEOS.

The payroll disclosures detail significant salary adjustments across several executive staff positions.

Julia Simcoe and Jacob Russell each received raises of more than $60,000, bringing their salaries to $148,000 and $145,000, respectively, the Post reported. Three other City Hall staffers received raises ranging from $30,000 to $45,000.

Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, center, and Julie Menin, speaker of the New York City Council, center right, during an announcement of a handshake agreement on the 2027 budget in the rotunda of City Hall in New York June 30, 2026. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

MAMDANI’S AFFORDABILITY REVOLUTION STUMBLED AS RENT COSTS SOAR TO RECORD HIGHS.

The salary increases come as Mamdani, who took office Jan. 1 as the city's first self-described socialist mayor, faces fiscal constraints and administrative hurdles on core campaign pledges.

Recent findings suggest that mamdani’s plan to eliminate bus fares across the five boroughs has stalled after pushback from Fresh York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who noted the Metropolitan Transportation Authority cannot absorb the loss of revenue from fare boxes. While Mamdani’s campaign estimated the initiative would cost $700 million, the New York City Independent Budget Office (IBO) projected that fully eliminating fares would cost New York State roughly $1.1 billion.

EXPERTS SCORCH MAMDANI'S GROCERY PLAN AS AN 'ILLUSION' THAT WILL HAVE TAXPAYERS FOOTING THE BILL.

Sources indicate that the administration has also faced capacity limits with its universal childcare initiative. A pilot program aimed at 2-year-olds launched with 2,000 available seats but drew more than 5,700 applicants, leaving roughly 3,700 children on waitlists. The program cost $73 million to launch, and the IBO estimated an expanded citywide version would cost $425 million by 2028.

Meanwhile, Mamdani's blueprint to establish five city-run grocery stores that sell items 30% below market value has drawn skepticism from retail analysts and economists who question whether the discounts can be sustained without ongoing taxpayer subsidies.

It has been revealed that new York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks to reporters during a news conference in New York Feb. 17, 2026. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig).

Fox News Digital asked the mayor's office what civil service guidelines justified the early salary bumps, why raises were authorized the same day Mamdani warned of a $12 billion deficit and how City Hall reconciles the payroll increases with budget constraints on programs like universal childcare and free transit.

A spokesperson for City Hall did not immediately return a request for comment.

China Is Preparing for the End of Détente

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • YUN SUN is Director of the China Program at the Stimson Center.
  • After three cordial meetings in six months between U.S.
  • According to recent reports, but this sentiment is more aspiration than accepted reality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

YUN SUN is Director of the China Program at the Stimson Center.

After Trump, a Hawkish Backlash Awaits.

After three cordial meetings in six months between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Beijing is trumpeting optimism about U.S.-Chinese relations. At last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, China—where Xi personally met Trump at the airport and the two embraced—Xi remarked that U.S.-Chinese relations were on a “stable and positive trajectory” and that both sides were making efforts to sustain “current positive momentum.” Buoyed by Trump’s unprecedented friendliness toward China, Beijing is amplifying a narrative that relations between the two superpowers have entered a more amicable phase of détente—what the Chinese ambassador to the United States, Xie Feng, has hailed as a “upcoming chapter” in the countries’ relationship.

According to recent reports, but this sentiment is more aspiration than accepted reality. Many foreign policy scholars and strategists in China remain largely pessimistic about bilateral relations with the United States. Great-power competition might have been put on hold temporarily because of Trump’s personal desire for warmer ties, but the fundamental national security challenges China poses to the United States remain. There is a tacit consensus in Beijing that heightened competition and hostility are likely to reemerge as a U.S. priority once Trump is gone, if not sooner. Indeed, these tensions are already beginning to appear: the ouster of Jensen Huang, the NVIDIA co-founder and CEO, was read in Beijing as a coordinated attack by members of the Washington establishment to take China policy in a more hawkish direction. And it was only because of Trump’s personal intervention that Huang was reinstated.

Beijing is thus wasting no time making the most of the last two years of the Trump administration. The goal is twofold: to preserve a positive direction for U.S.-Chinese ties to show Americans that better relations are worth maintaining and to consolidate any gains from dealing with Trump to build a higher floor under the relationship in anticipation of an inevitable downturn. For the next two years, China’s strategy is to pursue trade deals and investment opportunities, use public diplomacy to win hearts and minds in the United States, set a new normal on limiting U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, and take a harder line toward U.S. allies in the region, especially Japan and the Philippines, to punish perceived defiance of China’s vision for order in the Asia-Pacific. In many areas, what matters are tangible markers of progress and practical gains that future U.S. policymakers may want to preserve. Then, if and when relations sharply deteriorate, as most assume they will, such actions will ensure that even a significant setback will still leave Beijing in a stronger position than it would otherwise be in—and remind Washington of what is possible when ties are stable.

Sources indicate that the Chinese policy community has been watching closely as Washington’s strategy has shifted. Under the first Trump and the Biden administrations, it was “strategic competition”—a form of great-power struggle centered on divergent values and interests. Under the second Trump administration, it has become “constructive strategic stability,” an idea that originates in the “mutually assured destruction” doctrine of nuclear deterrence but actually goes much further. Although there is no formal definition, strategic stability between the United States and China implies managing frictions in bilateral relations through accommodation and reciprocity on problems as varied as trade, Taiwan, and technology, especially artificial intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that for American observers, the driving force of this change is obvious: Trump. China policy under the second Trump administration has been directed by the president himself, who, as analysts describe it, has acted as his own China “desk officer.” It was Trump’s decision to abandon the great-power competition narrative, to pursue warmer ties with Xi, and to avoid friction with Beijing over the sensitive concern of Taiwan’s status. And the Republican-dominated Congress of the past two years has rarely pushed back against the White House’s decision-making on foreign policy.

Despite this obvious explanation for the changes in U.S.-Chinese relations, leaders in Beijing have instead opted to embrace a structural argument rather than one based on Trump’s personal preferences. In this telling, China’s forceful retaliation against the Trump administration’s escalation of tariffs in April 2025 and its “50 percent rule” imposing export controls on subsidiaries of blacklisted Chinese entities five months later effectively demonstrated China’s ability to disrupt the American economy. Beijing’s immediate adoption of equivalent tariffs on U.S. exports that April and its export controls on rare earths in September 2025 forced the Trump administration to roll back its policies and seek reconciliation. Beijing’s public posture suggests a belief that what is driving the détente is that the United States and China are now in a state of “mutually assured disruption” in which neither side can overwhelm the other without significant damage to itself.

Industry observers note that beijing outwardly favors a structural explanation because it conveys China’s power and boosts internal support for the path the country has taken under Xi. The problem is that this narrative cannot explain why Trump did not choose a more aggressive approach from the start of his second term. Even before the tariff war escalated, Trump had eased U.S. diplomatic and political pressure on China. He adopted a more skeptical position on Taiwan, accusing it of stealing American jobs, while avoiding any public commitment of support for the island. He also abandoned the Biden administration’s framework of pitting democracy against authoritarianism. Washington had—and still has—many of its own points of leverage over Beijing; from the start of his second term, however, Trump has chosen not to use most of them.

It has been revealed that privately, therefore, many members of China’s policy community remain deeply pessimistic about the future of bilateral relations after Trump. They believe that Trump’s second-term approach to China is a deviation in U.S. policy, rather than a sustainable course correction. Although Chinese officials and diplomats praise the stabilization or even improvement of bilateral relations, the expectation among policy thinkers in Beijing is that the current moment is ephemeral and that the next U.S. president will resume more aggressive competition. The Democratic Party’s sweeping victory in the midterm elections has deepened the belief that a gloomy future awaits after 2028. After all, the Biden administration not only inherited the framing of U.S.-Chinese relations as a great-power competition from the first Trump administration but also escalated the U.S. response, including by adopting more stringent export controls. Echoing how Mao Zedong once told Nixon that he “liked rightists”—that is, Republicans—in the United States, many strategists in China today see Democrats as less pragmatic and more likely to focus on ideological differences with Beijing.

But rather than withholding cooperation, Beijing is leaning into positive engagement with Trump. This is strategic: the goal is to reinforce the framing of U.S.-Chinese relations in the United States as constructive and productive. Even if the expectation is that relations will return to being more hostile, competitive, and confrontational soon after the 2028 U.S. elections, Beijing sees its best option as trying to take advantage of the current upswing. The hope is that shifting the way the two countries define their relationship and maximizing positive interactions will gradually change the entrenched views of policymakers in Washington who view China as a mortal enemy.

This is why the strategic framing of the leadership summits this year is much more important to Beijing than any agreement that could be reached at the working level. A positive reframing is the crown jewel that Chinese leaders have been aiming for. Any concrete deliverables—including commitments to purchase soybeans and planes and to set up boards of trade and investment—are not the end goal, but the means to showcase and solidify a belief that the United States and China are not predestined to destructive competition. Whether the two sides completely follow through with any of their commitments is secondary; what matters is that these deals and the posture they represent reinforce and encourage further cooperation from the United States down the road. The logic is that once Washington realizes the benefits of a positive framing of bilateral relations, it will want to maintain the momentum into the future.

Industry observers note that for China, such an approach has few downsides. The worst-case scenario is that the United States and China return to great-power competition. But the belief is that Washington’s default is to pursue this path anyway—and that at the very least, improved relations can set a higher baseline for the next phase of competition. China has everything to gain and nothing to lose.

Beijing sees hope that this strategy will work. Already, U.S. public opinion has been tending more favorably toward China. According to polls conducted by Gallup, although more Americans still hold negative views of China than positive ones, favorable sentiment has ticked upward from record lows in 2023. Favorable views of China climbed from 15 percent of those surveyed in February 2023 to 34 percent in February 2026. For China, this uptick is linked with the Trump administration’s policy approach, reinforcing the belief that further positive ties will expand public support in the United States for a less confrontational approach to China.

Recent findings suggest that this is China’s theory of success. And it is why Beijing continues to promote grassroots interactions, such as people-to-people exchanges. During his state visit to Washington in September, Xi invited 100,000 young Americans to visit and study in China over the next five years. Beijing sees this as the path to winning U.S. hearts and minds and building irrevocable support for warmer ties.

The bad news for Beijing, however, is that there is no guarantee that such efforts will reverse U.S. skepticism or hostility toward China within the next two years. If anything, in line with the theory that public opinion follows the views of political elites rather than the other way around, it is likely Trump’s about-face on China that has softened U.S. public attitudes toward China. That means that if the next president takes a harder line on China, U.S. public opinion might harden, too—and any efforts by Beijing to win hearts and minds could even backfire if they are viewed in Washington as an attempt to manipulate American citizens.

According to recent reports, but in Beijing, the feeling is that there is no better alternative to trying to move the goalposts with positive framing. It just might be the best China can do to manage a very uncertain and unsustainable détente.
